title: The Planck Wall
detail: Not the beginning so much as the edge of what physics is currently able to say. Above roughly 10³² degrees, gravity and the other three forces are expected to merge and spacetime itself to become grainy and uncertain — and every theory we possess stops returning answers. What lies earlier is not unknown so much as, for now, unaskable.
evidence: This is where our theories stop, not where the evidence stops. The Planck scale is not measured but derived: it is the only way to combine the gravitational constant, Planck's constant and the speed of light to get a length, a time and an energy. The claim being made is about the failure of general relativity and quantum field theory when used together, which is a statement about our equations rather than about the rock.

title: Inflation
detail: In a sliver of a sliver of a second, space expands by something like a factor of 10²⁶ — a proton swelling to the span of a galaxy. It flattens the universe, dilutes whatever came before to nothing, and stretches quantum jitter into the faint density ripples that will, much later, become every galaxy there is.
evidence: Inflation was proposed to fix three things the plain Big Bang cannot explain: patches of sky that have never been in contact with one another are the same temperature to one part in a hundred thousand; space is flat to within a fraction of a percent; and the magnetic monopoles the theory expects are nowhere to be found. The positive evidence is the pattern of ripples in the microwave background, whose distribution across angular scales matches stretched quantum fluctuations — including a slight tilt away from perfect uniformity that was predicted before it was measured.

title: The Forces Divide
detail: The Higgs field settles into place and the electroweak force splits in two, into electromagnetism and the weak force. From this instant onward the universe runs on exactly the four forces we still measure today, and particles carry mass for the first time.
evidence: One of the very few moments in the early universe that can be recreated on demand. Electroweak theory predicted the W and Z bosons together with their masses, and both were found at CERN in 1983; the Higgs boson followed in 2012. The energy at which the forces separate is not inferred from the sky at all — it is read off collider experiments.

title: The Quark–Gluon Plasma
detail: Far too hot for quarks to hold on to one another, so matter exists as a plasma with almost no viscosity — the most perfect fluid known. Heavy-ion colliders at CERN and Brookhaven now recreate droplets of it, a few thousand particles at a time, lasting about 10⁻²³ of a second.
evidence: Made in the laboratory. RHIC and the LHC smash gold or lead nuclei together and produce droplets of the stuff lasting around 10⁻²³ of a second. Its near-zero viscosity is read from elliptic flow: in an off-centre collision the debris streams out more strongly along one axis than the other, and how strongly depends on how freely the plasma flowed. That it behaved as a liquid rather than a gas was not what anyone expected.

title: Matter Wins by a Whisker
detail: Quarks bind into protons and neutrons, and then matter and antimatter annihilate each other almost completely. For every billion pairs that vanish into light, roughly one particle of ordinary matter is left standing — and that residue is every atom in every star, planet and body that will ever exist.
evidence: The size of the surplus is measured rather than assumed. The ratio of photons to surviving matter particles follows from the ripple pattern in the microwave background, and independently from the amount of primordial deuterium; both give roughly a billion photons for every particle of matter left. Why there is any surplus at all is unexplained — the charge-parity violation known in particle physics is orders of magnitude too small to produce it.

title: Neutrinos Set Free
detail: One second in, the universe thins enough that neutrinos stop colliding with anything and fly off in straight lines. They are still passing through you — roughly 300 per cubic centimetre, cooled by expansion to under two kelvin, older than any light we will ever be able to see.
evidence: These neutrinos have never been detected directly and probably cannot be with current methods; they carry far too little energy. They show up instead as a contribution to the radiation density of the early universe, which shifts the positions of the peaks in the microwave background and alters how much helium is produced. Both measurements agree on three species streaming freely from about one second onward.

title: The First Elements
detail: For about twenty minutes the entire universe is a fusion reactor, and then it cools out of the window and the reactions stop. It leaves roughly three quarters hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass, with a trace of lithium — a ratio we still measure in the oldest stars, and one of the strongest pieces of evidence we have that this whole account is right.
evidence: The calculation has essentially one adjustable number — the density of ordinary matter — and from it predicts how much hydrogen, helium, deuterium and lithium should exist. Deuterium measured in gas clouds backlit by distant quasars fixes that number; helium measured in metal-poor galaxies then agrees without further adjustment. Lithium comes out about three times too high, and the disagreement has not been resolved.

title: Matter Overtakes Light
detail: Radiation has dominated the energy of the universe until now, but as space stretches, light loses ground faster than matter does. Gravity finally gets the upper hand, and the faint ripples left over from inflation can begin to deepen instead of being smoothed flat.
evidence: The crossover is written into the microwave background. Fluctuations that were small enough to start collapsing before it are damped relative to those that entered later, and the bend in the power spectrum where that behaviour changes gives the density of matter directly.

title: The Universe Turns Transparent
detail: Cooled to about three thousand degrees, nuclei finally capture electrons and light stops being endlessly scattered. That released light is still arriving — stretched by expansion into microwaves at 2.725 kelvin. It is the oldest image of anything, and nearly everything we know about the early universe is read off its faint mottling.
evidence: Found by accident in 1965 by Penzias and Wilson, who spent months hunting for the source of an unshiftable hiss in their antenna, including evicting a pair of pigeons and scrubbing out their droppings, before concluding it came from the sky. COBE later showed the spectrum is the most perfect blackbody ever measured. The temperature at earlier epochs has been checked independently by measuring how molecules are excited in distant gas clouds — hotter then, by exactly the predicted amount.

title: The Dark Ages
detail: No stars, no galaxies, no light at all beyond the fading afterglow — just cooling hydrogen fog drifting into the first faint clumps. It lasts something like a hundred million years, and it is the one long era for which we still have almost no direct observation of any kind.
evidence: Almost nothing here is observed. The era is bracketed rather than seen: the microwave background marks its beginning and the earliest galaxies its end, and the interval between is filled in by models. The one direct probe is the 21-centimetre line of neutral hydrogen; a claimed detection announced in 2018 remains disputed and has not been independently confirmed.

title: The First Stars
detail: With no heavier elements to help gas clouds shed heat and fragment, the first stars come out enormous — tens to hundreds of solar masses, burning blue-white, and dead inside a few million years. Not a single one has ever been observed. We know them only from the wreckage they left in the generation that followed.
evidence: Entirely inferred — not one has ever been seen, and none may ever be. The case rests on the chemistry of the oldest surviving stars in the Milky Way's halo, whose unusual element ratios match what models say a metal-free supernova should leave behind, and on a conspicuous absence: despite long searches, no star with zero heavy elements has ever been found, which is what you would expect if the whole generation was massive and short-lived.

title: The First Galaxies
detail: Clumps of dark matter draw in gas, and the first galaxies assemble — small, lopsided and furiously forming stars. JWST has now found one at redshift 14.3, shining when the universe was under three hundred million years old, and it is brighter and further along than the models had any right to expect.
evidence: Directly observed, and unusually solidly. JWST measures these redshifts spectroscopically, from the sharp break where intervening hydrogen absorbs the light, rather than estimating them from colours — a method that had produced several false records. That the galaxies are brighter and more built-up than the models allowed for is an open problem rather than a settled conclusion.

title: Reionization
detail: Ultraviolet light from the first stars and quasars strips the electrons back off the hydrogen fog, bubble by bubble, until the bubbles meet. Over several hundred million years the universe becomes clear again — the last time the entire cosmos changed state at once.
evidence: The end is dated by the Gunn–Peterson trough: quasars beyond redshift six have their light absorbed away entirely at wavelengths shorter than Lyman-alpha, which only happens if neutral hydrogen still lies between us and them. Nearer quasars do not show it. How long the whole process took is constrained separately by the amount of polarisation the microwave background picked up from scattering off freed electrons.

title: The Supermassive Black Holes
detail: Quasars driven by black holes of a billion solar masses are already blazing when the universe is under a billion years old — far too early to have been built up from ordinary dead stars. The leading explanation is that vast gas clouds collapsed straight into heavy seeds, skipping the star stage altogether.
evidence: Masses are read from the width of emission lines in the quasar's spectrum — faster-orbiting gas means a deeper gravitational well — combined with brightness, which cannot exceed the Eddington limit without blowing the fuel supply away. The problem is then arithmetic rather than observational: even growing flat out at that limit, a black hole starting from a dead star cannot reach a billion solar masses in the time available.

title: The Milky Way Assembles
detail: Our galaxy's thick disk is largely in place within the first billion years, and then it spends the next ten swallowing smaller galaxies whole. One meal alone — the Gaia-Enceladus collision — delivered around a quarter of the stars in the halo, and they are still recognisable today by the shape of their orbits.
evidence: Gaia has measured positions and motions for nearly two billion stars. Debris from a swallowed galaxy stays clustered in orbital energy and angular momentum long after it has smeared out in actual space, so old mergers can be found as clumps in that abstract space rather than as visible streams. Ages come from the chemistry and surface gravity of individual stars.

title: Cosmic Noon
detail: Star formation peaks about ten billion years ago, running roughly twenty times faster than it does today. Most of the stars that have ever existed were lit within this stretch — and the universe has been quietly winding down ever since.
evidence: Built by surveying galaxies at many different redshifts and measuring how fast each is forming stars, using ultraviolet light as the direct tracer and infrared emission from warmed dust to recover what the dust hides. Combining the surveys gives a single curve of star formation against cosmic time, which rises to a peak near redshift two and falls by roughly a factor of twenty to the present day.

title: The Sun Ignites
detail: A cold cloud in a spiral arm collapses, possibly nudged by a nearby supernova whose fingerprints survive as decay products in meteorites. Within a few million years the core reaches ten million degrees and fusion begins. The leftover two tenths of one percent of the disk becomes everything else.
evidence: The date is one of the most precise numbers in all of geology: lead-lead dating of calcium-aluminium inclusions in meteorites, the first solids to condense out of the disk, gives 4.567 billion years with an uncertainty of well under a million. The supernova trigger is inferred from the decay products of aluminium-26 and iron-60 in those same inclusions — both have short half-lives, so they must have been made shortly before the solar system formed and injected into it.

title: Earth Accretes
detail: Dust grains stick, pebbles clump, and inside about ten million years a planet's worth of rock has swept its own orbit clear. It is molten, airless and under constant bombardment — nothing about it yet suggests what it is going to become.
evidence: Core formation is dated by hafnium–tungsten isotopes, a clock that only runs during the planet's first fifty million years. The age of the Earth as a whole comes from lead isotopes, pinned down by Clair Patterson in 1956 using meteorites — work that required a laboratory clean enough to defeat the lead contamination that had defeated everyone before him, and which led him to discover how much lead industry had put into the environment, and to spend the rest of his career getting it out of petrol.

title: The Moon
detail: A body about the size of Mars strikes the young Earth, and the thrown-up debris settles into a ring and then into a moon, possibly within a century. It handed Earth its tilt, its tides, and a stabiliser for its axis — and it is still moving away from us, about 3.8 centimetres a year.
evidence: Lunar rock has oxygen isotope ratios essentially identical to Earth's, which rules out a body captured from elsewhere in the solar system, since composition varies with distance from the Sun. It is also strongly depleted in iron and in volatile elements, exactly as material blasted off a mantle after a core had already formed would be. The recession rate is not modelled but measured, by timing laser pulses bounced off reflectors the Apollo crews left behind.

title: The Late Bombardment
detail: The giant planets shift their orbits and fling debris through the inner solar system, cratering everything that will hold a scar. The Moon's dark maria are the wounds; Earth took the same beating and simply resurfaced itself, which is why the record survives up there and not down here.
evidence: Apollo samples dated by argon clustered suspiciously around 3.9 billion years, which was read as a spike in impacts. That reading has weakened considerably: the samples may all derive from a single large basin, biasing the clock, and revised dynamical models now favour a long declining tail of bombardment rather than a discrete late cataclysm. The cratering itself is not in doubt; its timing is.

title: Dark Energy Takes Over
detail: For nine billion years gravity has been gradually slowing the expansion. Then the thinning matter loses out to a constant pressure that appears to be built into space itself, and the universe begins to accelerate apart. The result was found in 1998 in the unexpected dimness of distant supernovae, and it remains the largest unexplained number in physics.
evidence: Type Ia supernovae explode at a consistent brightness once corrected for how fast they fade, so how faint one looks gives its distance. Two teams working independently found in 1998 that distant ones are dimmer than any decelerating universe permits. The result is now corroborated by two unrelated lines: the microwave background, and baryon acoustic oscillations — a fixed length frozen into the distribution of galaxies which can be used as a ruler at different epochs.

title: The Sun Brightens
detail: The Sun has been growing steadily more luminous for its whole life — roughly one percent every hundred million years, leaving it about thirty percent brighter now than when Earth formed. Why the young Earth was not frozen solid under that fainter sun is still an open question.
evidence: Not observed but calculated, and the calculation is tightly constrained. Stellar models must reproduce the Sun's measured mass, radius, luminosity and surface composition, and are checked against helioseismology — the Sun rings like a bell, and the frequencies depend on conditions all the way to the core. Given those constraints, brightening is unavoidable: as hydrogen becomes helium the core contracts and heats, and the output rises.

title: The Hadean Opens
detail: There is no landscape yet, only a surface. Earth is still being hit hard enough and often enough that the outer few hundred kilometres stay molten, and after the Moon-forming impact the whole planet is a magma ocean under an atmosphere of vaporised rock. The Moon hangs perhaps ten times closer than it does now and raises tides in liquid stone. The day is around six hours long. As the rock vapour rains out and the surface crusts over, the steam left in the air condenses, and it rains — for a very long time.
evidence: The timing of core formation comes from hafnium–tungsten isotopes, which only work as a clock during the first fifty million years. The Moon-forming impact is dated from Apollo samples. The magma-ocean stage is a model result rather than an observation: no rock of that age survives anywhere, because the surface was repeatedly remelted.
facts: Vaporised rock, then steam and CO₂

title: The Jack Hills Zircons
detail: Grains of zircon barely wider than a human hair, weathered out of long-vanished rocks and buried in a much younger sandstone in Western Australia. They are the oldest pieces of Earth anyone has ever held, and they carry a chemical signature that should not be there so early: the magma they crystallised from had already been mixed with cool liquid water.
evidence: Uranium–lead dating of the crystals themselves gives ages up to 4.404 billion years. Their oxygen-18 content is higher than mantle values, which happens when rock is altered by liquid water near the surface at low temperature. That pushes oceans, and a crust to hold them, back to within 150 million years of the planet's formation.

title: The Late Veneer
detail: When Earth's core formed it should have taken essentially all the gold, platinum and iridium down with it, because those metals dissolve readily in iron. The mantle has far more of them than that allows. The surplus was delivered afterwards, by roughly half a percent of an Earth mass of leftover debris arriving after the core had closed. Every gold atom in every ring was added late, and never sank.
evidence: The argument is entirely a mass balance: measured mantle abundances of the highly siderophile elements against what metal–silicate partitioning experiments say should remain. Their relative proportions match chondritic meteorites, which points at ordinary leftover planetesimals rather than anything exotic.
facts: Excess Au, Pt, Ir in the mantle

title: The Archean Opens
detail: A blue-water ocean covering most of the planet, broken by volcanic islands and a few small patches of proto-continent that barely clear the waves. There is no free oxygen at all. The sea holds dissolved iron and would look faintly green; the sky is probably not blue but orange, hazed by an organic smog produced when sunlight works on methane. The Sun is only about three-quarters as bright as it is now, and the fact that the oceans are not frozen is still not fully explained.
evidence: Sulfur isotopes are the strongest line: without an ozone layer, ultraviolet light splits sulfur dioxide in a way that leaves a mass-independent fingerprint. It is present in every rock older than about 2.4 billion years and absent afterwards, which brackets an atmosphere with essentially no oxygen. Pillow-shaped lavas at Isua show eruption under water, and banded iron formations require iron to have been dissolved in the sea, which only happens without oxygen.

title: The Acasta Gneiss
detail: A banded, folded grey rock on an island in the Slave craton of northwest Canada, and the oldest intact piece of Earth's crust known — not a loose crystal but an actual outcrop you can put a hand on. The boundary between the Hadean and the Archean is now formally drawn at its age, which makes this rock the definition of the eon rather than merely a specimen from it.
evidence: Uranium–lead dating of zircons within the rock. The interpretation is delicate: the gneiss has been metamorphosed repeatedly, so the ages come from cores of crystals that survived the reheating while their rims record later events.

title: The Last Universal Common Ancestor
detail: Not the first living thing, but the one whose descendants are the only ones left. It already had DNA, a genetic code identical to ours, ribosomes, ATP, and a membrane it pumped ions across — several hundred genes' worth of machinery that every organism alive still runs on. Everything since, from oaks to whales to the bacteria in your gut, is a variation on a cell that lived somewhere around four billion years ago.
evidence: Nothing is fossilised here. LUCA is reconstructed by comparing the genomes of living organisms and keeping whatever all three domains share, then dating the split with molecular clocks calibrated against fossils further up the tree. Estimates cluster between about 4.2 and 3.9 billion years, and the error bars are wide enough to matter.

title: Isua
detail: A belt of battered, cooked, folded rock in southwest Greenland that is nonetheless still recognisably sedimentary and volcanic — pillow lavas that erupted under water, and banded iron laid down in a sea. Some of the carbon in it is unusually light, in the way that carbon fixed by living cells is light, which would make it the oldest chemical trace of life. Whether it really is has been argued for fifty years.
evidence: Pillow structures show underwater eruption directly. The life claim rests on carbon isotopes in graphite grains: biological carbon fixation prefers carbon-12, leaving a signature that can also, unhelpfully, be produced by some purely chemical reactions at high temperature — which is exactly what these rocks have been through.

title: The Oldest Stromatolites
detail: Layered domes and cones of sediment in the Pilbara of Western Australia, built up millimetre by millimetre as microbial mats trapped grains and grew over them. They are not fossils of bodies but fossils of behaviour — the shape a community of microbes makes when it keeps reaching for the light. Living ones still grow in Shark Bay, a few hundred kilometres away.
evidence: The case is structural rather than chemical: the laminations wrinkle and thicken in ways sediment does not do on its own, and the cones point in directions that track light rather than current. Abiotic look-alikes exist, so each candidate is argued individually.

title: Oxygenic Photosynthesis
detail: Some cyanobacterium works out how to break a water molecule instead of a weaker donor, and gains an inexhaustible supply of electrons in exchange for a waste product that is violently reactive. For hundreds of millions of years the oxygen goes straight into dissolved iron and rock and never reaches the air. Then the sinks fill up.
evidence: The date is contested by half a billion years. The strongest arguments are indirect — traces of oxygen-dependent chemistry in rocks well before the atmosphere changed, sometimes called whiffs, and the phylogeny of the photosynthetic machinery itself.
facts: Oxygen sunk into iron and rock

title: The Continents Come Up
detail: Continental crust has been forming for a long time, but around now enough of it is thick and buoyant enough to stand permanently above sea level. For the first time there is properly dry land in quantity: bare, unweathered, lifeless, and immediately exposed to rain that begins stripping nutrients off it and washing them into the sea.
evidence: Read from strontium and hafnium isotopes in seawater-derived rocks, which shift when rivers start delivering material weathered from old continental crust. Shale chemistry changes at the same time, in a way that only makes sense if subaerial weathering had begun in earnest.
facts: Sr and Hf isotopes, shale chemistry

title: The Paleoproterozoic Opens
detail: Real continents now, gathered into the first supercontinents and worn down by rain and rivers into plains of bare rock and sand — a landscape that would look almost ordinary except that there is nothing growing on any of it. The sea is still iron-green and the air still has no oxygen worth the name. Both are about to change, and the change will nearly end life on Earth.
evidence: Continental configurations at this depth come from palaeomagnetism: iron minerals lock in the direction of the magnetic field as they cool, giving each block a latitude and orientation that can be matched against others. Sedimentary rocks show mature, well-sorted sands, which take large stable landmasses and long rivers to produce.

title: The Great Oxidation
detail: The iron and rock that had been absorbing oxygen for hundreds of millions of years finally saturate, and it starts accumulating in the air. To almost everything then alive, oxygen is a poison, and this is very likely the largest extinction in the planet's history by proportion of life killed — carried out by life, as pollution. It is also the reason any large, energetic organism became possible.
evidence: The cleanest marker is negative: the mass-independent sulfur isotope signature, which needs an ozone-free sky, vanishes from the record between about 2.45 and 2.32 billion years ago and never returns. Red beds — sandstones stained by oxidised iron — appear at the same time, and banded iron formations largely stop.

title: The Huronian Glaciation
detail: Methane is a far stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and the new oxygen destroys it. The planet loses much of its insulation and freezes, in a series of glaciations lasting on and off for roughly three hundred million years — the longest cold period Earth has ever had, and quite possibly the first time ice reached the equator.
evidence: Tillites — the unsorted rubble that only glaciers leave — occur in the Huronian Supergroup north of Lake Huron and on several other continents, sandwiched in the section immediately above the oxidation signal. Palaeomagnetic data put some of those deposits at low latitude.

title: The Lomagundi Excursion
detail: The largest and longest swing in carbon isotopes in the entire rock record, lasting over a hundred million years. It records organic carbon being buried on an enormous scale, which means oxygen being released on an enormous scale — possibly to levels near today's. Then it ends, and oxygen falls back to a fraction of a percent for the next billion years.
evidence: Measured directly as carbon-13 enrichment in marine carbonates worldwide, reaching values around +10 per mil against a baseline near zero. The oxygen implication follows from the carbon budget: burying reduced carbon leaves the oxygen behind.

title: The Francevillian Biota
detail: Centimetre-scale discs and lobed shapes in black shale in Gabon, more than a billion years before anything else that size. If they are organisms they are the oldest large multicellular life by an enormous margin; if they are mineral growths they are a very good imitation. The debate has run since they were described in 2010 and is not resolved.
evidence: They are made of pyrite in shale, with consistent shapes, size distributions and a sulfur isotope composition that fits microbial sulfate reduction. Against that, purely chemical processes can grow pyrite into disc shapes, and no cellular structure has been found in any specimen.

title: The Cell Inside the Cell
detail: One cell takes in another and does not digest it. The swallowed bacterium keeps its own membrane and its own DNA and goes on producing energy, and its host gets a power supply it did not have to build. Every plant, animal and fungus is descended from that one event, and your mitochondria still carry a small circular genome that is more closely related to some free-living bacteria than to you.
evidence: The evidence is molecular and structural rather than fossil: mitochondria have their own circular DNA, double membranes, bacterial-type ribosomes, and divide independently of the cell. Their gene sequences place them squarely inside the alphaproteobacteria.

title: The Mesoproterozoic Opens
detail: The most uneventful stretch in Earth's history, and it lasts a billion years. No glaciations anywhere. No large swings in the carbon cycle. Oxygen sits at perhaps a hundredth of today's level and does not move. The supercontinent Nuna is assembled, its interior a vast stony desert with sand seas and braided rivers and, near water, mats of cyanobacteria that would look like green stains on the rock. Eukaryotes exist but stay small and rare. Geologists call it the Boring Billion, and the interesting question is why nothing happened.
evidence: This period is characterised by absences, which are harder to argue than presences: no glacial deposits are known on any continent, and the carbon isotope curve, measured in thousands of samples, runs flat. Low oxygen is inferred from chromium isotopes and from the scarcity of trace metals like molybdenum in black shales.
facts: Bare rock and sand; microbial crusts

title: The Sulfidic Ocean
detail: With a little oxygen at the surface and none at depth, the mid-ocean fills with dissolved hydrogen sulfide. That strips iron and, more importantly, molybdenum out of the water — and molybdenum is what the enzyme that fixes nitrogen needs. The suggestion is that the ocean was nitrogen-starved for a billion years, and that this is why complex life sat still for so long.
evidence: Iron speciation in shales distinguishes oxygen-free water that is sulfidic from oxygen-free water that is not. Molybdenum concentrations in black shales stay low through the interval and rise afterwards. The link to nitrogen limitation is a hypothesis built on that chemistry, not a measurement.

title: Rodinia Assembles
detail: Continents collide along what is now the eastern edge of North America and throw up a mountain chain on the scale of the Himalaya, running for thousands of kilometres. The result is Rodinia, a single landmass holding most of the planet's continental crust, with an interior so far from any coast that it may have been one of the driest places the Earth has ever had.
evidence: Reconstructed from palaeomagnetic pole paths, which say where each block sat, and from matching the ages and chemistry of mountain belts that were later torn apart — the Grenville front in Canada continues into Scandinavia and beyond.

title: Bangiomorpha
detail: A branching filament of cells from Arctic Canada, and the oldest fossil that can be placed confidently inside a group still alive — it is a red alga, closely comparable to Bangia growing on rocks today. It is also the oldest direct evidence of sex, because it has differentiated spores, and of complex multicellularity, because its cells are specialised by position.
evidence: Identification is morphological and unusually secure: the fossils preserve cell-by-cell detail, including the characteristic wedge-shaped divisions and a holdfast, matching living Bangia closely. The age comes from rhenium–osmium dating of the shale it sits in.

title: The Tonian Opens
detail: Rodinia is at its greatest extent and beginning to crack. The land is still stone, but the stone is no longer sterile — microbial and algal crusts hold parts of it, enough to change how quickly rock weathers. The sea is clearing as sulfide retreats, oxygen is edging upward, and in the plankton something important happens: algae start displacing bacteria as the base of the food chain, and a mouthful of food becomes worth several times more than it used to be.
evidence: The plankton shift is read from biomarkers — the fatty molecules that survive in oil and shale. Steranes come from eukaryotic algae and hopanes from bacteria, and the sterane share climbs sharply through this period. Rodinia's break-up is dated from rift-related volcanic rocks along the new margins.
facts: Rodinia at maximum, starting to rift

title: The Rise of the Algae
detail: For most of Earth's history the open ocean ran on bacteria, which are small, and small food supports short food chains. As eukaryotic algae take over, each mouthful carries far more carbon and energy, and it becomes possible to make a living by eating things that eat things. Nothing large exists yet, but for the first time the energy budget allows it.
evidence: Sterane-to-hopane ratios in sedimentary rocks and oils, which record the relative contribution of eukaryotes and bacteria to buried organic matter. The rise is sharp and appears in basins on several continents, which argues against it being a local or preservational artefact.

title: The Vase-Shaped Microfossils
detail: Flask-shaped shells a tenth of a millimetre across, with a single neat opening, found by the thousand in the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon and elsewhere. They are testate amoebae — single-celled predators that built a house and hunted from it. Some specimens have circular holes punched through the wall, which is the oldest direct evidence of one eukaryote eating another.
evidence: The shells match those of living testate amoebae in shape, size and aperture design closely enough for confident assignment. The predation claim rests on the holes being consistently round, of consistent size, and placed as a hunting organism would place them rather than where the shell is weakest.

title: Rodinia Breaks Up
detail: The supercontinent splits, and the pieces spread out around the tropics. That matters more than it sounds: fresh basalt weathering in equatorial rain consumes carbon dioxide, and there is now a great deal of new coastline and new rock in exactly the wettest, warmest place to put it. The planet's thermostat is being turned down, and the Cryogenian is next.
evidence: Dated from the flood basalts and dyke swarms that mark continental rifting, and from palaeomagnetic latitudes placing the fragments near the equator. The weathering argument is supported by strontium isotopes in seawater, which shift as more continental material is delivered to the ocean.

title: The Cryogenian Opens
detail: Rodinia is splitting apart along the equator, and the fresh basalt it exposes weathers in the tropical rain, pulling carbon dioxide out of the air faster than volcanoes can put it back. There is nothing on land but rock, dust and a varnish of microbes near water; everything that lives, lives in the sea. The planet is about to cool past the point where ice makes more ice, and stay there.
evidence: Rodinia’s position at the equator comes from palaeomagnetism in the rift-related lavas. That bare land was nonetheless weathering fast is read from strontium isotopes in seawater, which record how much continental material rivers were delivering. The absence of anything living on land is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, but no body fossil or root trace of any kind occurs in terrestrial rocks of this age.

title: The Sturtian Snowball
detail: Ice reaches the equator and stays there for something like fifty-seven million years — the longest glaciation in Earth's history, with the ocean possibly sealed under a kilometre of it. Life survives somewhere, and what emerges on the far side is more complicated than what went in.
facts: To sea level at the equator

title: The Ediacaran Opens
detail: The ice has just gone. Meltwater pours off a scoured planet and floods the ocean with the rock flour the glaciers ground out. The continents are low and scattered, drowned around their edges by warm shallow shelves; behind the shoreline the land is still bare stone under a sky far richer in carbon dioxide than ours. For the first time the deep ocean begins to hold oxygen — and within fifty million years there will be things living in it big enough to see without a lens.
evidence: The thaw is dated from the cap carbonate that sits directly on the glacial rubble, and from uranium–lead ages on ash beds within it. Deep-ocean oxygenation is inferred from iron speciation and from rare-earth patterns in the carbonates. That the land was bare rests on the same negative record as before, plus the absence of the clay minerals that soil-forming processes produce.
facts: Hothouse, straight out of a glaciation

title: The Marinoan Thaw
detail: The second global glaciation ends, and the meltwater lays a sheet of pale carbonate straight over the glacial rubble on every continent. That contact is the formal base of the Ediacaran — the last period before animals, defined by the moment the ice let go.

title: The Weng'an Embryos
detail: Phosphate in southern China preserves individual cells — clusters of two, four, eight, sixty-four, dividing exactly the way an animal embryo divides. Whether they are animals, or something else that happened to cleave the same way, has been argued over for thirty years and is not settled.

title: The Gaskiers Glaciation
detail: A short glaciation — under a million years, brief by the standards of what came before it. Directly above the deposits it left in Newfoundland lie the first large, complex organisms in the fossil record, which is either the most important coincidence in the history of life or not a coincidence at all.

title: Charnia
detail: A fern-like frond built from branches that branch into smaller copies of themselves, all the way down — a body plan with no living descendant and no obvious mouth. It was found in an English quarry by schoolchildren, one of whom was told in 1956 that fossils do not occur in rock that old. It reopened the Precambrian.

title: The Avalon Assemblage
detail: Ash from a volcano settles over a deep-sea community and buries it where it stood — thousands of organisms across Newfoundland bedding planes, each one still in life position. They lived below the depth sunlight reaches, so none of them were photosynthesising, and how they fed is still unknown.

title: Something Moves
detail: Shallow grooves a few millimetres wide that start, stop, and change direction. Nothing drifting leaves a track like that; something is choosing where to go. It is the oldest evidence of an animal with a front end and a reason to use it.

title: Dickinsonia
detail: A flat ribbed oval, up to a metre and a half across and only millimetres thick, which left a trail of feeding impressions behind it as it moved. In 2018 cholesterol was recovered from one of the fossils — a molecule only animals make — ending a forty-year argument about whether the Ediacarans were animals at all.

title: Kimberella
detail: A bilaterally symmetrical body with what looks like a shell, found with fans of scratch marks raked into the sediment ahead of it. Something was scraping a microbial mat with a hard structure at its front end — the oldest evidence anywhere of one organism eating another.

title: The First Skeletons
detail: Millimetre-wide tubes of calcium carbonate, grown as a stack of nested cones — the first hard parts anything ever built. Some of them have neat round holes bored clean through the wall, which means that by the time the first skeleton existed, something had already worked out how to get past it.

title: Namacalathus
detail: A calcified goblet on a stalk, growing in reefs alongside Cloudina in what is now Namibia. Recent work on the chemistry of its shell recovered animal-type molecules, placing at least one of the first skeleton-builders firmly among the animals.

title: The Ediacaran Ends
detail: The boundary with the Cambrian is drawn not at an extinction or a change of rock but at a burrow: the first appearance of Treptichnus pedum, a complex probing trace made by an animal working through the sediment rather than over it. Almost none of the Ediacaran body plans cross the line.

title: The Cambrian Opens
detail: Stand anywhere on land and nothing in sight is alive — no soil, no roots, no green, just rock, sand and a crust of microbes where there is water. Rivers do not have banks the way ours do; with no roots to hold sediment they spread into wide braided sheets and wander across the plain. Gondwana is assembling in the south while Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia sit apart near the equator, and warm shallow seas have flooded far inland across all of them. There is no ice at either pole, and there will not be for another ninety million years.
evidence: Continental positions come from palaeomagnetism and from matching faunas across what were then separate oceans. The flooded interiors are read straight from the rock: shallow-marine limestones and sandstones sit far inside every continent. The braided-river claim comes from channel geometry — pre-vegetation river deposits are consistently wide, shallow and sheet-like, and they change shape permanently once plants arrive.
facts: Barren rock, no plants or soil

title: The Small Shelly Fauna
detail: For twenty million years the rock is full of millimetre-scale cones, tubes, plates and spines in enormous numbers, most of which cannot be attached to any animal at all. Many are now thought to be single scales off larger creatures that fell apart after death — armour with no owner. Whatever they were, building with minerals had stopped being unusual.

title: The First Animal Reefs
detail: Archaeocyaths — sponge-grade animals shaped like a perforated cup sitting inside another perforated cup — cement themselves together on shallow carbonate platforms and build the first reefs made by animals rather than by microbial mats. They spread worldwide within a few million years and are essentially gone by the end of the Early Cambrian, leaving reef-building to be invented again from scratch.

title: The First Trilobites
detail: Trilobites arrive already finished: a hardened three-lobed shell and compound eyes built from hundreds of calcite lenses, each grown as a single crystal aligned to its optical axis. They are mineral optics, and the oldest eyes we know of that could form an image. Trilobites go on to be the most abundant fossil on Earth for the next two hundred and seventy million years.

title: The Chengjiang Biota
detail: Fine mudstone in Yunnan holds gills, guts, eyes and even nervous tissue in animals that had no hard parts whatsoever. More than two hundred and fifty species have come out of it, and because it is ten million years older than the Burgess Shale it shows the Cambrian fauna already assembled rather than in the act of assembling.

title: Anomalocaris
detail: A metre-long swimmer with a ring-shaped plated mouth, a pair of grasping appendages at the front and rows of flexible flaps down each side — the largest animal of its age by a wide margin, and the first predator big enough to make being small a strategy. Its parts were described as three separate creatures, including a jellyfish and a shrimp, before anyone realised they belonged to one animal.

title: The First Vertebrates
detail: Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys, from the same Chengjiang mudstones, are two or three centimetres long, with a stiffening rod down the back, a distinct head, gill arches and V-shaped blocks of muscle along the flanks. They are the oldest animals built to our plan, and everything with a backbone since is a variation on it.

title: The Burgess Shale
detail: A slurry of mud slides off the edge of a carbonate platform, buries a whole community and seals it away from oxygen. Charles Walcott found it in British Columbia in 1909 and collected some sixty-five thousand specimens. The animals in it were so unlike anything alive that several were given phyla of their own, and arguing about where they belong occupied palaeontology for most of the century that followed.

title: Hallucigenia
detail: Reconstructed for decades as a creature walking on stilt-like spines with a row of tentacles waving from its back, then turned over when better specimens showed the spines were armour and the tentacles were pairs of legs. The head was sorted out last: the blob everyone had taken for one turned out to be decay fluid squeezed out of the other end.

title: Pikaia
detail: A flattened five-centimetre swimmer from the Burgess Shale with a stiffening rod running its length and blocks of muscle either side of it. It is a chordate, and for most of the twentieth century it was presented as our own ancestor — until Chengjiang produced animals ten million years older that were already further along than it was.

title: The SPICE Event
detail: A sharp swing in carbon isotopes records a burst of organic burial and a spread of oxygen-poor water up onto the continental shelves. Trilobite faunas are cut down repeatedly through the Late Cambrian, and each time the handful of survivors radiates back out into the space that has just been cleared.

title: The Ordovician Opens
detail: Sea level is among the highest it has ever been, and shallow water covers the continents to a degree difficult to picture: much of what is now North America, Europe and China lies under a warm sea a few tens of metres deep, clear enough to see the bottom. Gondwana stretches from the tropics across the South Pole. Carbon dioxide is perhaps fifteen times modern levels and the world is hot. The land is still bare — but not for much longer, and the first things to colonise it will help wreck the climate that made this world possible.
evidence: Sea level is reconstructed from the geometry of sedimentary sequences, which record shorelines advancing and retreating across the continents. Continental positions come from palaeomagnetism and from the distribution of faunas that could not cross deep ocean. Carbon dioxide estimates come from the density of stomata on later plants, from carbon isotopes in soil carbonates, and from models tied to weathering rates.
facts: Near the highest in the record

title: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification
detail: Over roughly twenty-five million years the number of marine genera roughly triples, and the cast of the ocean changes permanently. The Cambrian fauna of trilobites and odd stem-groups gives way to brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, corals and cephalopods — animals that filter, encrust and build, filling the water column and the seafloor in ways nothing had before. It is the largest sustained expansion of diversity in the fossil record.
evidence: Counted directly, from occurrence databases compiling hundreds of thousands of fossil records by stage and region. The pattern survives correction for the obvious biases — more rock of some ages than others, more collectors working some regions than others — which is what makes it convincing rather than merely apparent.

title: The First Land Plants
detail: The oldest evidence is not a plant but its spores: clusters of four, walled in a decay-resistant polymer, blown or washed into marine sediments in Oman. The plants themselves were probably liverwort-grade — low, flat, rootless mats hugging damp ground. Small as they are, they begin the slow work of turning rock into soil, and of pulling carbon dioxide out of the air fast enough to cool the planet.
evidence: Cryptospores in Ordovician marine rocks, identified by their tetrad arrangement and by wall chemistry matching land-plant sporopollenin rather than algal material. Body fossils do not appear for another thirty million years, so the plants are inferred entirely from what they shed.

title: The Ordovician Meteor Event
detail: An asteroid roughly a hundred and fifty kilometres across is destroyed by a collision in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, and for the next few million years Earth is showered with the debris — a flux of meteorites perhaps a hundred times the normal rate. Swedish limestone quarries cut through fossil meteorites at a rate that would be unbelievable in rock of any other age.
evidence: More than a hundred fossil meteorites have been recovered from a single quarry system in Sweden, dated by the marine fossils enclosing them. Their chromite grains identify them as L-chondrites, and cosmic-ray exposure ages show they spent only a short time in space before arriving — consistent with a single recent break-up.

title: The Giant Orthocones
detail: Straight-shelled cephalopods, related to the modern nautilus, grow to several metres — the largest animals on the planet and the first to be big and mobile at once. The shell is divided into gas-filled chambers threaded by a tube that lets the animal adjust its buoyancy, so a creature the length of a canoe could hang motionless in the water and then move under jet propulsion.
evidence: Known from abundant body fossils; the chambers and the connecting siphuncle are preserved directly in cross-section. Buoyancy control is inferred by comparison with living Nautilus, which uses the identical arrangement. Reported maximum sizes vary because most specimens are incomplete.

title: Armour Before Jaws
detail: Jawless fish plated in bone — a head shield, a slot for a mouth, and a muscular tail. They cannot bite, only suck and filter, but they have solved something else first: bone, grown as external armour long before it was ever a skeleton. The teeth in your head are descended from the same tissue, still built the same way, in the same layers.
evidence: Body fossils with mineralised dermal plates preserving the microscopic layering of dentine and enamel-like tissue. That these are the same tissues as our teeth is a histological identification, made by sectioning the fossils and comparing structure directly rather than by any inference from the gross form.

title: The Hirnantian Glaciation
detail: Gondwana is sitting over the South Pole, and the new plants weathering the continents have drawn down enough carbon dioxide to tip the balance. Ice sheets spread across what is now the Sahara, sea level drops by around a hundred metres, and the vast shallow seas that held most of the world's life simply drain away. Around eighty-five percent of species die. It is the second-largest extinction in Earth's history, and the only one caused by cold.
evidence: Glacial striations and tillites are preserved across North Africa, in some places as pavements scoured by ice that can still be walked on. Sea-level fall is read from the sedimentary record on every continent. The extinction is counted from occurrence data, and oxygen isotopes in fossil shells record the temperature drop directly.

title: The Silurian Opens
detail: The ice is melting and the sea is coming back, drowning the continental interiors again within a few million years. What follows is one of the warmest, most stable stretches in the whole Phanerozoic — no ice at either pole, and shallow clear water over most of the flooded land. Laurentia and Baltica are closing on each other and raising a mountain chain along the join. And on the wet edges of the land there is now, for the first time, something green: low mats and tufts of plant a few centimetres high, hugging the ground beside water.
evidence: Sea-level rise is read from sedimentary sequences that step landward across every continent. The absence of ice is inferred from oxygen isotopes in fossil shells and from the lack of glacial deposits anywhere of this age. The mountain building is dated from the metamorphism and granites of the Caledonian belt, which can still be traced from the Appalachians through Ireland and Scotland into Norway and Greenland — a single chain torn apart much later by the Atlantic.
facts: Warm and unusually stable; no polar ice
First vegetation, low and near water

title: The Reefs Come Back
detail: After the Hirnantian, reef-building restarts and then overshoots. Tabulate and rugose corals grow alongside stromatoporoid sponges into structures tens of metres thick, and the Silurian ends up with some of the most extensive reef systems in the record — the limestone of Gotland and of Wenlock Edge in Shropshire is what is left of them.
evidence: Read directly from the rock: the reef masses are preserved in growth position, with the framework organisms still where they grew and the debris aprons fanning off their flanks in the correct direction. Their extent is mapped by tracing the limestone bodies across outcrop and borehole.

title: The Caledonian Collision
detail: The Iapetus Ocean finishes closing and Laurentia collides with Baltica, welding North America, Greenland, Scandinavia and what will become Britain into a single continent. The mountains thrown up along the suture are Himalayan in scale, and the sand and gravel stripped off them makes the Old Red Sandstone that floors much of northwest Europe. Scotland and England were on opposite sides of that ocean and were joined here.
evidence: The suture is mapped from the rocks either side of it, which carry entirely different fossil faunas of earlier age — animals that could not cross a deep ocean. Ophiolites, slices of ocean floor caught in the collision, mark the join itself. The timing comes from radiometric dates on the metamorphism and on the granites intruded during and after the squeeze.
facts: Laurussia, the Old Red Sandstone continent

title: Cooksonia
detail: A few centimetres tall, forking in twos, with a knob of spores at the tip of each branch — no leaves, no roots, no flowers, nothing to admire. What matters is inside: a strand of reinforced cells running up the stem that carries water against gravity and holds the plant up. Every tree that has ever existed is an elaboration of that strand.
evidence: The identification as a vascular plant rests on thin sections showing thickened conducting cells in the stem, not on the shape alone. Sporangia are preserved at the branch tips, which is what separates these from algae washed in from elsewhere.

title: The First Air-Breather
detail: A millipede a centimetre long, found in a sandstone at Stonehaven on the Aberdeenshire coast, and the oldest known animal that unambiguously breathed air. The evidence is a row of small holes along its side — spiracles, which open into a tracheal system and are no use whatsoever underwater. The land had plants on it; now something was living on them.
evidence: Spiracles are visible directly on the cuticle of the specimen under magnification, and they are the diagnostic feature: a gill-breathing arthropod does not have them. The age has been revised more than once as the host rocks were re-dated, and is now placed in the Late Silurian rather than earlier.

title: The Sea Scorpions
detail: Eurypterids reach their peak here — armoured arthropods with paddles at the back for swimming and, in the large predatory kinds, a pair of spined grasping claws at the front. Some are the size of a dog and the largest to come are over two metres, which makes them the biggest arthropods that have ever lived. Many were living in brackish and fresh water, close to the edge of the land.
evidence: Known from abundant, often superbly preserved body fossils, including moults, which are far commoner than corpses and can be told apart by how the plates are splayed. Size estimates for the giants come from isolated claws scaled against complete smaller specimens, which is why the numbers carry a margin.

title: Plants Grow Leaves
detail: Baragwanathia has stems clothed in narrow spirally arranged leaves, and roots below — a lycopod, recognisably the same design as the clubmosses growing in damp woodland today. Leaves are a solar panel, and once plants had them the amount of energy they could capture, and the rate at which they could break down rock into soil, changed by an order of magnitude.
evidence: Preserved as compressions in Australian siltstone with the leaf arrangement and vascular strand intact. The age has been contentious for a century, because the graptolites used to date the beds imply an earlier appearance than the plant record elsewhere allows; the dispute is about correlation rather than about the fossil.

title: The Origin of Our Jaw
detail: Entelognathus, from Yunnan, is a placoderm — an armoured fish from a group thought to be a dead end — but its face carries the same three jaw bones found in every bony fish, and in every land vertebrate down to you. Before it was described in 2013, those bones were assumed to be an invention of the bony fish lineage. It moved the origin of our own jaw into a group nobody expected.
evidence: The argument is anatomical and specific: the specimen preserves a maxilla, premaxilla and dentary in an otherwise unambiguous placoderm skull. Guiyu, from beds of similar age, provides the complementary evidence from the bony-fish side. Both are articulated rather than isolated bones, which is what makes the comparison possible.

title: The Devonian Opens
detail: Laurussia sits across the equator, hot and seasonal, shedding red sand off the Caledonian mountains into braided rivers. The land is green now, but only just: knee-high at the tallest, crowded along water, with soil no more than a few centimetres deep. Over the next sixty million years that changes more than in any comparable stretch before or since. Plants work out wood, and height, and deep roots, and by the end of the period there are forests thirty metres tall standing on real soil — and the carbon dioxide they have pulled out of the air has cooled the planet enough to bring ice back to the poles.
evidence: The continent is reconstructed from palaeomagnetism and from the Old Red Sandstone itself, which is the same distinctive red river deposit in Scotland, Norway, Greenland and eastern North America. Soil depth is measured directly from palaeosols — fossil soils, identifiable by their root traces and weathering profiles, which get thicker and more structured up through the section. The carbon dioxide fall is tracked by the density of stomata on fossil leaves, which plants adjust according to how much is available.
facts: Hot and seasonal; CO₂ falling fast
Forests 30 m tall, ice at the poles

title: The Rhynie Chert
detail: A hot spring in Aberdeenshire repeatedly floods a boggy patch of ground with silica-saturated water, and the whole ecosystem is turned to glass where it stands. Plants are preserved upright with their internal cells intact; so are mites, springtails, a spider relative and the fungi in the plant tissue. It is the earliest terrestrial ecosystem we can examine organism by organism rather than infer.
evidence: Silica permineralisation replaces tissue cell by cell without collapsing it, so thin sections show cell walls, spore contents and even fungal filaments inside plant roots. The plants are in growth position with rhizomes attached, which proves the community is preserved where it lived rather than washed together. A specimen long claimed as the oldest insect was reinterpreted in 2020 as something else, and the earliest definite insect is now younger.

title: The Zachelmie Trackways
detail: Footprints in a Polish quarry, made by something with four limbs and distinct digits walking on a tidal flat. They are around eighteen million years older than the oldest tetrapod skeleton anyone has found, and older than the fish that were supposed to be the tetrapods' immediate ancestors. Published in 2010, they pushed the whole sequence back and left a long stretch of the story with tracks in it but nothing to make them.
evidence: The prints preserve manus and pes impressions in alternating sets with digit marks, which rules out fish fin-drags or invertebrate traces. The age comes from conodonts in the enclosing marine beds, which date the horizon tightly. The tension with the body-fossil record is real and unresolved: trace fossils record behaviour we have no bones for.

title: The First Forest
detail: At Gilboa in New York State, a flood buries a stand of trees and preserves their bases where they grew. They are Wattieza, eight metres tall, with a crown of frond-like branches and no leaves as we would recognise them — closer to a tree fern than to anything living. Quarrymen turned up the stumps in the 1870s; the crowns that go with them were not found until 2004.
evidence: The stumps sit upright on a single bedding plane with their root flares intact, which is what distinguishes a forest floor from a raft of driftwood. Matching the crowns to the bases required finding both in the same beds, which is why the reconstruction took more than a century.

title: Archaeopteris
detail: The first tree that would look like a tree: a woody trunk up to a metre across, proper branches, flat green leaves, and roots going metres down. It reproduced by spores like a fern but built its wood like a conifer, and it spread across every continent, forming the first forests dense enough to shade a forest floor. Wood is the reason: a rigid pipe that holds water columns under tension and lets a plant get above its neighbours.
evidence: Trunks and foliage were described as two different fossils for a century — the wood as Callixylon, the leaves as Archaeopteris — until a specimen was found in 1960 with both still attached. Growth rings in the wood record seasonality; the depth of the associated root traces is read from palaeosols.

title: Roots Break the Rock
detail: Deep roots do something no earlier plant could: they prise rock apart mechanically and dissolve it chemically, metres below the surface. That accelerates the weathering that draws carbon dioxide out of the air, and it flushes phosphorus and nitrogen into rivers on a scale the oceans had never dealt with. The result is algal blooms, water stripped of oxygen, and — very probably — the extinctions that punctuate the rest of the period. The forests are the cause of the crisis.
evidence: Palaeosols thicken and develop deep root traces through the Middle and Late Devonian, which dates the change directly. The nutrient link is modelled rather than measured, but it is supported by the timing of black shale deposition, by nutrient proxies in those shales, and by carbon isotope records tracking the drawdown.

title: Tiktaalik
detail: A flat-headed predator a couple of metres long with eyes on top of its skull, gills and lungs, scales and fin rays — and inside its front fins, a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist. It could prop itself up. It also had something no fish has: a neck, because the skull had come free of the shoulder girdle, so it could turn its head to look at something instead of turning its whole body.
evidence: This one was predicted before it was found. The team reasoned that the transition should lie in freshwater rocks of Late Devonian age exposed at the surface, consulted a geological map, picked Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic, and spent four summers there before the fossils turned up in 2004. A prediction that specific, paying off, is about as strong as palaeontological evidence gets.
facts: Shoulder, elbow, wrist, and a neck

title: The Kellwasser Event
detail: Two pulses of extinction close together at the end of the Frasnian, recorded worldwide as black, organic-rich mudstone laid down in water with no oxygen in it. Reef systems are hit hardest of all: the great stromatoporoid and coral reefs of the Devonian collapse and are not rebuilt on that scale for a hundred million years. Warm-water shallow marine life suffers far more than anything in cold or deep water.
evidence: The two black shale horizons can be traced between continents and correlated by conodont zones, which is what shows this is a global event and not a local basin going stagnant. The anoxia is read from iron speciation and trace metals in the shales; the selectivity of the losses comes from counting which groups disappear where.

title: Acanthostega
detail: A tetrapod with four proper limbs, and eight fingers on each hand. It also had internal gills and a fin down its tail, and its limbs could not have held its weight on land. That combination settled an old argument in the opposite direction from what everyone assumed: legs did not evolve for walking out of water. They evolved in the water, for moving through weed and shallow debris, and were only later found to be useful on land.
evidence: Ellesmere and East Greenland material collected in 1987 preserved articulated limbs, which earlier finds had not. The digit count is read directly from the specimens. The gill argument comes from grooved bones in the throat that support internal gill bars, and the limb-strength argument from the geometry of the joints, which do not allow the postures walking requires.

title: Dunkleosteus
detail: An armoured placoderm with no teeth at all — instead, the jaw bones themselves are drawn out into shearing blades that sharpened each other every time the mouth closed. The bite is among the most powerful ever calculated for a fish, and the jaw could open in a fraction of a moment, pulling prey in with the inrush of water. It was the last great predator of a group that had ruled the seas for eighty million years and was about to vanish entirely.
evidence: Only the armoured head and shoulder region fossilises well; the rest of the body was cartilaginous and is not preserved, which is why length estimates have been revised repeatedly and recently reduced. Bite force is computed from the lever geometry of the reconstructed jaw muscles, so it is a calculation from anatomy rather than a measurement.

title: The Hangenberg Event
detail: The Devonian closes with a second crisis, and this one falls on vertebrates. The placoderms go completely — an entire class, gone, after eighty million years. Most lineages of early tetrapods and lobe-finned fish disappear with them, and the survivors pass through a bottleneck so narrow that the vertebrate world on the far side looks fundamentally different: it is the ray-finned fish and the sharks, and a handful of tetrapods, that inherit everything.
evidence: Marked by a global black shale and by a sharp drop in vertebrate diversity counted across well-sampled sections. Glacial deposits in South America of the same age indicate a short severe ice phase, consistent with the carbon drawdown the forests had been driving. Sea-level fall is read from the sedimentary record on several continents.

title: The Mississippian Opens
detail: Warm, clear, shallow sea over most of Laurussia — so shallow and so clear that the seafloor is a meadow. Crinoids stand on segmented stalks in dense gardens, filtering with feathery arms, and when they die their stems fall apart into millions of little discs. Enough of them accumulate to make whole mountains: the limestone of the Peak District, the Burren and the Mississippi valley is largely the wreckage of these animals. On land the forests are recovering from the Devonian collapse, and ice is quietly beginning to build on Gondwana.
evidence: The crinoid meadows are not reconstructed but counted: thin sections of these limestones are made of crinoid ossicles, and the fabric shows them broken in place rather than transported far. Sea depth and clarity follow from the carbonate itself, which requires warm shallow water. The southern ice comes from tillites and striated pavements in South America, southern Africa and Australia.

title: Romer's Gap
detail: For about fifteen million years after the Devonian there are almost no tetrapod fossils anywhere. It was named for the palaeontologist who noticed it, and for decades it was taken as a real event — a bottleneck, or a stretch when low oxygen held vertebrates back. Then people went and looked properly in Scottish and Nova Scotian rocks of exactly that age, and started finding them. The gap has been shrinking ever since.
evidence: This is a case study in how an absence gets misread. The gap correlated with a scarcity of suitable exposed rock and with a collecting tradition that had not targeted it. Once a project deliberately sampled Tournaisian sediments in the Scottish Borders, tetrapods, lungfish and arthropods came out of them. What is left of the gap is now much narrower, and is still narrowing.

title: Pederpes
detail: A metre-long tetrapod from Dumbartonshire whose feet point forwards. That sounds trivial and is not: the Devonian tetrapods had paddle-like limbs splayed sideways, useful in water. A foot that points the way the animal is going is a foot built to push against ground. This is close to the oldest evidence of a vertebrate that actually walked.
evidence: Read from the articulation of the ankle and the asymmetry of the foot skeleton, which distinguish a forward-facing stance from the sprawling paddle arrangement. The specimen sat misidentified as a fish in a museum collection for years before being recognised and redescribed in 2002.

title: The Seed
detail: A spore is a single cell that must land somewhere wet. A seed is an embryo packed with food and sealed in a coat, which can wait, and travel, and germinate somewhere a spore would die. The earliest known seeds are latest Devonian, but it is here that seed plants spread away from water and start colonising ground that was previously off-limits. Every conifer, oak and grain crop is downstream of this.
evidence: Fossil ovules are identified by their integument — a protective layer wrapped around the megaspore with a gap left at the top for pollen. That structure is visible in compression fossils and in permineralised material, and it separates true seeds from the spore-bearing plants they evolved from.

title: The Age of Sharks
detail: With the placoderms gone, cartilaginous fish inherit the sea and diversify into shapes that have never been repeated. Stethacanthus carries a flat-topped structure on its back like a shaving brush, covered in enlarged denticles, and has a matching patch on its head; nobody knows what it was for. This stretch has more disparity of shark body plan than any time since.
evidence: Sharks are mostly cartilage and rarely fossilise whole, so the record is dominated by teeth and denticles — which is why diversity here is measured largely in tooth morphology. A handful of exceptional sites, particularly Bear Gulch in Montana, preserve whole bodies with soft tissue, and it is those that show the strange ones.

title: The Long Ice Age Begins
detail: Ice sheets spread across the southern half of Gondwana and stay for something like eighty million years — the longest icehouse of the last half-billion years, and the only one before our own that a land vertebrate lived through. Sea level begins swinging by tens of metres as the ice grows and melts, and those swings will end up written into the coal seams of the next period as a repeating rhythm.
evidence: Glacial deposits, striated pavements and dropstones across South America, southern Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia — the same sequence on each, which is one of the observations that first suggested those continents had been joined. The timing is fixed by the marine fossils in the beds above and below.
facts: Sea level swinging tens of metres

title: The Pennsylvanian Opens
detail: A belt of waterlogged lowland forest runs right around the equator, across what will become eastern North America and northern Europe. The trees are not trees as we know them: they are giant clubmosses fifty metres tall, held up by a thick photosynthetic bark rather than by wood, standing in standing water on roots that barely go down. Horsetails the width of a person grow in the wetter parts. There are no flowers, no grass, no birdsong, and no animal in the canopy larger than an insect. Oxygen is at the highest level in the planet's history, and the air is thick enough that fires burn through wet swamp.
evidence: The vegetation is known in extraordinary detail because coal balls — lumps of mineralised peat — preserve the plants cell by cell, and because whole stumps stand upright in the roof shales of coal seams. The high oxygen comes from geochemical models of the carbon and sulfur cycles, and is supported by charcoal in the coals themselves, which records repeated wildfire in an environment far too wet to burn under present-day air.
facts: Lycopsids to 50 m, held up by bark

title: Lepidodendron
detail: A trunk like a column of green scales, each diamond the scar of a shed leaf, growing as an unbranched pole for most of its life and only forking into a crown at the very end — after which it reproduced and died. It reached fifty metres in perhaps fifteen years, held up almost entirely by its outer bark, with a spongy interior and a shallow forked root system. Most of the world's coal is the compressed remains of these.
evidence: Growth strategy is read from the anatomy: very little wood, a huge bark cylinder, and no evidence of the branch scars that a tree growing a crown throughout its life would leave. Coal balls preserve the internal tissue directly. The species were named separately for their trunk, bark, roots, leaves and cones before anyone realised they belonged to one plant.

title: The Egg That Left the Water
detail: At Joggins in Nova Scotia, lycopsid stumps stand upright in the cliff face, and inside some of them are the bones of small lizard-like animals that fell in and could not get out. Hylonomus is among the oldest known reptiles, and its significance is not the animal but the egg: a membrane-wrapped private pond that lets an embryo develop on dry land. Every reptile, bird and mammal since has that egg, or a modification of it.
evidence: The egg itself does not fossilise this early. Amniote status is inferred from skeletal features that go with it — the shape of the skull, the ankle, the absence of the larval characters amphibians retain. Joggins was central to nineteenth-century geology: Lyell visited, and he and Dawson found the first specimens inside the hollow stumps in 1852.

title: Arthropleura
detail: A millipede two and a half metres long and half a metre wide — the largest land invertebrate that has ever lived, and by a wide margin. It has no known predators of comparable size and appears to have been a plant-eater working through the leaf litter. A single fragment of one, found weathering out of a sandstone block on a Northumberland beach in 2018, was enough to revise the size estimates upward.
evidence: Complete specimens are unknown; the animal is reconstructed from partial trunk segments and from its trackways, which are preserved as parallel rows of small prints up to fifty centimetres apart. Diet is inferred from plant fragments found in the gut region of some specimens, though the identification is disputed.

title: Why There Is So Much Coal
detail: About a fifth of all the coal ever formed was laid down in this one period. The famous explanation is that trees had invented lignin and fungi had not yet invented how to digest it, so dead wood simply piled up unrotted for sixty million years. It is a beautiful story and it may not be right: the counter-argument is that the coal is mostly bark rather than wood, that fungi capable of the job appear earlier than the hypothesis needs, and that what really mattered was tectonics — vast subsiding equatorial basins, kept wet, in exactly the wrong place to dry out.
evidence: The fungal hypothesis was dated by molecular clock in 2012, placing lignin-degrading white rot near the end of the Carboniferous. The challenge, from 2016, comes from re-examining what the coals are made of and from the geological setting of the basins. Both sides are working from the same seams; the disagreement is about what the seams mean.
facts: Lignin before the fungi to rot it

title: The Glacial Rhythm
detail: Cut through the Pennsylvanian anywhere in the coal belt and you get the same sequence over and over: marine limestone, then shale, then a coal seam, then sandstone, then limestone again. Each cycle is the shoreline sweeping in and out as ice grows and melts on Gondwana, thousands of kilometres away. Some sections contain a hundred of them stacked up. The wobble of Earth's orbit is legible in a wall of rock.
evidence: The cycles are correlated between basins on different continents, which rules out local subsidence as the cause. Their thicknesses and durations, once dated, come out at the periods of orbital eccentricity and precession — the same Milankovitch beats that drove the recent ice ages, recorded three hundred million years earlier.

title: The Oxygen Peak
detail: Oxygen reaches somewhere around a third of the atmosphere, the highest it has ever been, because carbon is being buried faster than it is being returned. Denser, richer air lets insects push their tracheal breathing further than it has ever gone before or since, and the giants of this period are the direct consequence. It also means that almost anything will burn: charcoal is common in the coals, in swamps that should have been too wet to ignite.
evidence: Estimated from geochemical models of the long-term carbon and sulfur cycles, cross-checked against the isotopic composition of sedimentary sulfides and organic carbon. The independent physical check is charcoal abundance, since sustained fire has a lower oxygen limit that can be tested experimentally.

title: Meganeura
detail: A predatory insect with a wingspan of about seventy centimetres — the size of a large bird, hunting in the air above the swamps. It is not a dragonfly but a griffinfly, a related order that is entirely extinct. Insects breathe by letting air diffuse down branching tubes rather than by pumping it, which puts a hard ceiling on body size; in this thicker air, that ceiling was much higher.
evidence: Known from wings, which preserve far better than bodies, so wingspan is measured directly while body mass is estimated. The oxygen explanation is supported experimentally: insects reared in oxygen-enriched air grow larger over generations, and tracheal dimensions scale as the argument predicts.

title: The Rainforest Collapse
detail: The climate dries, and the continuous belt of coal forest breaks into isolated patches. The giant lycopsids largely disappear and are replaced by tree ferns; amphibian diversity, tied to standing water, falls sharply and does not recover. Reptiles, carrying their water with them inside an egg, do the opposite — the fragmentation isolates populations, and they diversify. It is the first extinction event known to have been caused by the loss of a habitat rather than by a catastrophe.
evidence: Read from the plant record in the coal measures, where lycopsid spores drop out and fern spores take over across the belt. The tetrapod pattern comes from occurrence databases, corrected for the fact that the coal swamps were themselves an unusually good preservation environment — losing the swamps could mimic losing the animals, and separating those two effects is the hard part.

title: The Permian Opens
detail: Every continent has joined. Pangaea runs from pole to pole in one piece, wrapped in a single world ocean, and its interior lies thousands of kilometres from any coast. That interior is desert on a scale the Earth has not had before or since — dune fields the size of countries, salt flats, seasonal rivers that go nowhere. Summers and winters swing violently because there is no sea nearby to moderate them. The coal swamps are gone; conifers and seed ferns take the dry ground, and on it the synapsids — our own lineage — become the first large land animals.
evidence: Pangaea is reconstructed from palaeomagnetic latitudes, from mountain belts that match across the Atlantic, and from fossils: the seed fern Glossopteris occurs on every southern continent, and no seed crosses an ocean.
