The deserts are read directly from the rock, since wind-blown dunes leave steep cross-bedding at angles water cannot produce, preserved in the Coconino and Rotliegend sandstones. The extreme seasonality comes from climate models of a supercontinent and is confirmed by growth rings in fossil wood.
facts: Pangaea — one landmass, pole to pole

title: Glossopteris
detail: A tongue-shaped leaf from a seed fern that grew across the whole southern half of Pangaea. Its significance is not the plant but its distribution: identical leaves occur in South America, southern Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, and a seed fern cannot cross an ocean. Wegener used exactly this to argue for continental drift and was disbelieved for fifty years. Scott's polar party were hauling sixteen kilograms of Glossopteris-bearing rock when they died; the fossils were found with the bodies.
evidence: The argument is biogeographic and simple: the same species, in the same beds, on continents now separated by thousands of kilometres of deep ocean, with no dispersal mechanism that could account for it. Antarctic specimens were the closing piece, because they placed the flora on the continent that sits at the centre of the reconstructed fit.

title: Dimetrodon
detail: The animal that ends up in every dinosaur toy set and is not a dinosaur — it died out some forty million years before the first one existed, and it is more closely related to you than to any reptile alive. The sail is a row of enormously extended vertebral spines; what it was for is still argued. Its teeth are the point: different shapes doing different jobs in one jaw, which is a mammalian trait, and its name means two measures of tooth.
evidence: Its position on our side of the tree comes from the skull, which has a single opening behind the eye — the synapsid condition — rather than the two that reptiles and birds have. That single hole is the diagnostic feature, and it is visible in every specimen. The sail's function is inferred from bone histology and surface area calculations, which have supported thermoregulation, display and structural support at different times.

title: The Sand Seas
detail: Dune fields spread across the tropics of Pangaea, and in places their surfaces are preserved intact. The Coconino Sandstone in Arizona holds hundreds of trackways of small reptiles walking up dune faces, with the sand slumping behind each foot exactly as dry sand does. You can tell which way the wind was blowing three hundred million years ago, and which way the animal was going, from the same slab.
evidence: Wind-blown sand is distinguishable from water-laid sand by the steepness and scale of its cross-bedding, by the frosted rounding of the grains, and by their sorting. The trackway evidence is experimental: researchers walked living lizards across dry and damp sand at various slopes and matched the resulting slump patterns against the fossils.

title: The Therapsids
detail: Synapsids become something recognisably more like us. Gorgonopsians hunt with sabre-like canines; dicynodonts crop vegetation with a beak and two tusks; some have a secondary palate, which lets an animal chew and breathe at the same time. Bone texture in the snout suggests whiskers, which would mean hair. Nothing here is a mammal, but almost every part of the mammal is present somewhere in this group.
evidence: The mammalian traits are read from anatomy one at a time: differentiated teeth from the jaw, a secondary palate from the roof of the mouth, an upright limb posture from the hip and shoulder joints. Whiskers are the weakest of these, inferred from foramina in the snout that would carry nerves — a pattern that also occurs in some living reptiles, so it is suggestive rather than settled.

title: The Capitanian Crisis
detail: A distinct extinction eight million years before the famous one, and for a long time it was lumped in with it. Reef systems and large marine invertebrates are hit hard, and on land the biggest dicynodonts disappear. It coincides with the Emeishan flood basalts erupting through what is now southwest China — a smaller rehearsal, by the same mechanism, for what is coming.
evidence: Separating it from the end-Permian required dating the two events precisely enough to tell them apart, which only became possible with high-precision uranium–lead dating of ash beds. Once separated, the extinction shows up as its own step down in diversity counts, with the Emeishan basalts dated to the same interval.

title: The Siberian Traps
detail: The largest volcanic event in the rock record. Somewhere between three and seven million cubic kilometres of lava erupt across Siberia over perhaps a million years — enough to bury the continental United States half a kilometre deep. What makes it lethal is not the lava but what it erupted through: a basin filled with coal, oil shale and salt. The magma cooked all of it, and vented carbon dioxide, methane, sulfur and halocarbons straight into the atmosphere.
evidence: The lava pile is still there and can be measured and dated; uranium–lead ages on zircons put the main pulse within a few tens of thousands of years of the extinction horizon, which is a remarkably tight match. The role of the sediments is inferred from the intrusions themselves, from the composition of the gases trapped in them, and from a global mercury spike in rocks of exactly this age.

title: The Great Dying
detail: Around four fifths of marine species and perhaps seven in ten land vertebrates die. It is the closest life has come to being extinguished, and unlike the extinction that killed the dinosaurs there is no impact and no single moment — it is a chain: carbon dioxide, then warming of eight to ten degrees, then oceans too warm to hold oxygen, then acidification, then anoxic water spreading onto the shelves. Recovery takes five million years, which is far longer than any other extinction required.
evidence: The scale is counted from marine occurrence data across hundreds of sections. The temperature rise is measured from oxygen isotopes in conodont teeth, which are apatite and record seawater directly. Acidification is read from boron isotopes and from which shell chemistries fail. Anoxia comes from iron speciation and uranium isotopes. Four independent proxies, telling one story.

title: The Triassic Opens
detail: An emptied world, and a hot one. Sea surface temperatures in the tropics reach around forty degrees, which is lethal for most animals, and for several million years there is a band around the equator where large animals simply do not live — fish and reptiles are found north and south of it and not in it. Pangaea is still one continent and still mostly desert. There are no reefs. There is no coal being formed anywhere on Earth. Almost every ecological role is vacant, and the survivors that inherit them are not the ones that had been winning.
evidence: The temperatures come from oxygen isotopes in conodont apatite, sampled across latitudes, which is what revealed the equatorial gap; the fossil distributions independently confirm it. The absence of reefs and coal is a global negative in the sedimentary record — no reef limestone and no coal seam of this age is known anywhere, which is a much stronger statement than a local absence.

title: The Coal Gap
detail: For about ten million years no coal forms anywhere in the world. Coal requires peat, peat requires wetland plants growing faster than they rot, and the plants that had been doing that job were gone. It is the only interval in the last four hundred million years with no coal in it at all, and it is the clearest single measure of how thoroughly the land flora was destroyed.
evidence: An absence, but an unusually robust one: coal is economically valuable and therefore exhaustively mapped worldwide, so a global gap in the record is far less likely to be a sampling artefact than most absences are. The gap closes as new peat-forming plant communities assemble in the Middle Triassic.
facts: Only such gap since the Devonian

title: Lystrosaurus
detail: A barrel-bodied, beaked, tusked herbivore about the size of a pig, and for a while one of the most abundant land vertebrates that has ever existed. In parts of South Africa it makes up the overwhelming majority of tetrapod fossils in beds just above the extinction. It is not that Lystrosaurus won; it is that almost nothing else was left, and an empty world briefly belonged to a single unremarkable survivor. Its bones are found from Antarctica to Russia to China, which is also good evidence that those places were joined.
evidence: Dominance is measured by counting specimens in well-sampled bone beds rather than by species lists. The counts are corrected for the fact that a common animal in a good preservation setting will always look commoner than it was — but the effect here is far too large to be explained that way.

title: Back to the Sea
detail: Within a few million years of the extinction, land reptiles go back into the water and stay. Ichthyosaurs end up shaped almost exactly like dolphins — streamlined body, dorsal fin, crescent tail — despite being separated from dolphins by three hundred million years and a completely different ancestry. Some have eyes the size of dinner plates, the largest of any animal known, for hunting deep where the light fails. They give birth to live young, tail first, and there are fossils that died in the act.
evidence: Live birth is not inferred but observed: several specimens preserve embryos inside the body cavity, and at least one is preserved mid-delivery. Eye size is measured from the sclerotic ring, a bony hoop inside the eye that fossilises. The dolphin resemblance is the textbook case of convergent evolution, testable because the underlying skeletons are not alike at all.
facts: Live birth, preserved in the act

title: The Modern Reef
detail: Scleractinian corals appear — the stony corals that build every reef in the world today. The reef-builders of the Palaeozoic had all been destroyed, and this is a rebuild from a different starting point rather than a recovery. The partnership that makes coral reefs work, with photosynthetic algae living inside the coral's own tissue, is established somewhere around here, and it is what allows a reef to grow fast in water with almost no nutrients in it.
evidence: The corals are identified by skeletal microstructure, which differs from the extinct rugose and tabulate groups in a way that is visible in thin section. Whether the earliest of them already hosted symbiotic algae is argued from the carbon and oxygen isotopes of the skeleton and from growth-band spacing, and remains less certain than the corals themselves.

title: The Carnian Pluvial Episode
detail: For a million or two million years in the middle of a desert world, it rains. Arid sequences across several continents are interrupted by river and lake deposits, coal starts forming again, and then the dry conditions return. It coincides with a huge volcanic province erupting in what is now British Columbia. On the far side of it, dinosaurs are markedly more diverse and more abundant, and so are modern conifers — this looks like the door opening.
evidence: Recognised as a lithological change repeated on several continents, which rules out a local basin effect, and dated by conodonts and by radiometric ages on the associated volcanics. The link to dinosaur diversification comes from occurrence counts and from trackway abundance before and after, and is a correlation with a plausible mechanism rather than a demonstrated cause.
facts: Arid world becomes wet, then dries

title: The First Dinosaurs
detail: Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus, from the Ischigualasto badlands of Argentina — bipedal, lightly built, a metre or two long, and completely unremarkable members of their ecosystem. Dinosaurs do not take over on arrival. For the next thirty million years they remain a minority of land vertebrates, outnumbered by crocodile-line reptiles that were bigger, commoner and doing better. What they had was not superiority but, eventually, luck.
evidence: The Ischigualasto Formation is unusually well dated, with volcanic ash beds through the section giving radiometric ages directly tied to the fossils. Dinosaur status is established from the hip and ankle — an open hip socket and a particular ankle joint — which are the defining features, not size or posture.

title: The First Pterosaurs
detail: The first vertebrates to fly under their own power, a hundred million years before bats and seventy before birds. The wing is a membrane stretched from the body to the tip of a single, enormously elongated fourth finger — an entirely different solution from the feathered arm of a bird or the webbed hand of a bat. They appear in the record already fully capable of flight, with no intermediate stages known.
evidence: Flight capability is read from the skeleton: hollow bones with walls under a millimetre thick, an enlarged sternum for flight muscles, and the wing-finger itself. Membrane structure is known from rare specimens preserving soft tissue, which show reinforcing fibres running through it. The absence of intermediates is a genuine gap, not an interpretation.

title: The First Mammals
detail: Small, nocturnal, insect-eating, shrew-sized. Morganucodon would fit in a hand. What defines it is a rearrangement in the head: the reptilian jaw joint is replaced by a new one, and the two bones that had formed the old hinge shrink, detach, and migrate into the middle ear, where they become the malleus and incus. You are hearing this sentence with bones that used to be part of a jaw.
evidence: This is the best-documented major transition in the entire fossil record, because the therapsid sequence preserves it step by step: the new joint appears alongside the old one, both function together for a while, and then the old one is released. Some fossils have both jaw joints at once. Mammalian embryos still form the ear bones in the jaw region before they migrate, repeating the sequence.

title: The End-Triassic Extinction
detail: Pangaea begins to tear apart along the line where the Atlantic will open, and the rift erupts — the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, whose lavas are still found in Morocco, Portugal, Brazil and New Jersey. Around three quarters of species disappear. The crocodile-line reptiles that had been outcompeting the dinosaurs for thirty million years are almost entirely wiped out, and the dinosaurs, which are not, walk into an empty world.
evidence: The lava province is dated by uranium–lead and argon methods to within the extinction interval, and its four fragments are matched by chemistry across what is now the Atlantic. Carbon isotope excursions in marine sections mark the release of carbon; the loss is counted from marine and terrestrial occurrence data, and the differential survival of dinosaurs over pseudosuchians is read from tracking both groups through the same sections.

title: The Jurassic Opens
detail: Pangaea is coming apart. The rift that will become the Atlantic is opening, the Tethys seaway is widening from the east, and sea level rises until much of Europe is an archipelago of low limestone islands in warm shallow water. There is no ice at either pole and the world is humid and green — but a strange green: conifers, cycads, ginkgoes, tree ferns and horsetails, in a landscape with no flowers, no grass, and no broad-leaved trees. Nothing is coloured for pollinators, because there are none.
evidence: The break-up is dated from the rift basins along the eastern seaboard of North America and from the oldest oceanic crust preserved on either side of the Atlantic. Sea level is read from the extent of marine limestone across continental interiors. The flora is a direct fossil record of leaves, wood and spores; the absence of angiosperms is a global negative in a very well-sampled interval.
facts: Warm and humid; no polar ice
Conifers and cycads — no flowers, no grass

title: The Blue Lias
detail: A rhythmic stack of dark shale and pale limestone along the Dorset coast, laid down in a shallow anoxic sea and packed with ammonites, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs. Mary Anning, who lived on the beach at Lyme Regis and sold fossils to survive, found the first ichthyosaur skull anyone recognised at about twelve, the first complete plesiosaur, and the first British pterosaur. Her identifications were used, published and rarely credited; as a woman she could not join the Geological Society that relied on her.
evidence: The Blue Lias is one of the most intensively studied sequences in the world, its rhythms correlated bed by bed along the coast and tied to ammonite zones fine enough to divide the Early Jurassic into intervals of a few hundred thousand years. Anning's specimens are still the reference material for several species, which is why her work outlasted the credit she was denied.

title: The Atlantic Opens
detail: The rift stops being a rift and becomes an ocean: new crust starts being manufactured at a ridge in the middle, pushing the two halves apart at roughly the rate a fingernail grows. It has not stopped since. Every metre of Atlantic floor was made at that ridge and carried outward, which is why the ocean is youngest in the middle and oldest at the edges, and why there is no seafloor anywhere on Earth older than about 180 million years.
evidence: The proof is magnetic. As lava cools at the ridge it locks in the direction of Earth's field, and because the field reverses at irregular intervals the seafloor records a barcode of stripes — symmetrical on either side of the ridge, and matching the independently dated reversal sequence. Surveying those stripes in the 1960s is what turned continental drift from a suggestion into plate tectonics.

title: Chalk Begins
detail: A single-celled alga starts wrapping itself in interlocking plates of calcite. Coccolithophores are microscopic and there are more of them than almost anything, and when they die the plates rain down. For the first time carbonate accumulates on the deep ocean floor rather than only in shallow water — which permanently changes how the oceans handle carbon dioxide, giving them a buffer against acidification that they had never had before.
evidence: The plates are identifiable to species under a light microscope and are so abundant and fast-evolving that they are the standard tool for dating marine sediment cores. The change in ocean chemistry is inferred from where carbonate is deposited before and after: deep-sea carbonate is essentially absent from older rock and continuous afterwards.

title: Feathers Before Flight
detail: Small dinosaurs in what is now Liaoning are covered in feathers — not flight feathers, but branched, insulating down, on animals that could not fly and whose relatives never would. Feathers evolved for warmth, or for display, and were only later co-opted for flight, in the same way that limbs had evolved in water long before anything walked. We even know the colours: Anchiornis was grey with a red crest and black-and-white banded wings.
evidence: Colour comes from melanosomes — the pigment organelles — which survive as microscopic bodies in the fossil and whose shape determines hue in living birds. Sausage-shaped means black, spherical means reddish-brown. Mapping their shapes across a specimen and comparing against a reference library of modern feathers reconstructs the pattern. It was first done in 2010 and remains contested at the edges.

title: The Sauropods
detail: The largest animals ever to walk, several times the mass of any land mammal that has existed. They managed it by being full of air: the neck vertebrae are hollowed out by air sacs continuous with the lungs, which is a bird arrangement, so a thirty-metre animal could carry a neck it would otherwise be unable to lift. They did not chew — they stripped foliage and swallowed it, and let a vast fermenting gut do the work.
evidence: Pneumaticity is visible directly: sawn or scanned vertebrae are honeycombed with chambers that in living birds house air sacs. Mass estimates come from volumetric models built on mounted skeletons and cross-checked against limb-bone circumference, which predicts body mass reliably in living animals. Not chewing is read from the teeth, which show no grinding wear at all.
facts: No grinding wear — they did not chew

title: The Morrison Formation
detail: A band of river and floodplain sediment across the American West holding Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus — the dinosaurs of the popular imagination, nearly all from this one unit. It was excavated during the Bone Wars, a thirty-year feud between Cope and Marsh in which each hired crews to outdig the other, described specimens in reckless haste to claim priority, and on occasion dynamited sites rather than let the other have them.
evidence: The haste left a mess that is still being cleared: species named twice, skulls put on the wrong skeletons, and type specimens scattered between institutions. Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus were merged in 1903 on the basis of one such error and separated again in 2015 after a statistical reanalysis of the anatomy. The rock is excellent; it was the collecting that was bad.

title: The Solnhofen Lagoon
detail: A set of stagnant hypersaline lagoons behind a reef in southern Germany, where the bottom water held no oxygen and nothing lived to disturb what fell in. The lime mud is so fine that it preserves jellyfish, insect wings, the outlines of squid bodies, and the tracks of a horseshoe crab together with the animal that died at the end of them. The same stone was quarried for lithographic printing, which is why so much of it was split by hand and examined.
evidence: The absence of bottom-dwelling life in the beds, along with the salt and the fine even lamination, indicates water too saline and oxygen-poor for scavengers. Preservation this good is a function of that: soft tissue survives where nothing eats it and nothing stirs it. The trackway-with-carcass specimens are the direct demonstration that animals entering the lagoon did not last long.

title: Archaeopteryx
detail: Feathered wings, and also teeth, a long bony tail and clawed fingers. The first skeleton was described in 1861, two years after the Origin of Species, at a moment when the loudest objection to Darwin was the absence of intermediate forms — and here was an animal that was unarguably half of each. It is not the ancestor of birds, but it is the specimen that showed the category boundary was not real.
evidence: Twelve or so skeletons are known, all from Solnhofen, several with feather impressions preserved around the wings and tail. Its position has moved as more feathered dinosaurs have been found: it is now placed close to, and sometimes just outside, the line leading to modern birds. That reclassification does not weaken the original point — it strengthens it, by filling in the space around it.
facts: Feathers, and teeth, tail and claws

title: The Cretaceous Opens
detail: The continents are becoming recognisable but are in the wrong places: the South Atlantic is a narrow gulf, India is an island crossing an ocean on its own, and sea level climbs to the highest of the last half-billion years. Shallow seas cut North America in half and drown most of Europe. There is no ice anywhere, forests grow inside both polar circles and spend months of each year in darkness, and crocodile relatives live at latitudes that are now tundra. It is the warmest sustained world since animals existed.
evidence: Sea level is reconstructed from how far marine sediments reach inland on every continent at once, which cannot be produced by local subsidence. Temperature comes from oxygen isotopes in foraminifera and from organic membrane proxies in marine sediment. The polar forests are not inferred but excavated — fossil wood, leaf litter and growth rings from Alaska, Svalbard and Antarctica, with ring patterns showing months of continuous darkness.

title: The Flowers
detail: Angiosperms appear and then spread faster than any plant group ever has, until within about forty million years they dominate almost everywhere. A flower is a transaction: the plant pays an animal in nectar to carry pollen precisely, instead of releasing clouds of it and hoping. Fruit is the same deal for seeds. Darwin called their sudden appearance and rapid rise an abominable mystery, and the timing of their origin is still not settled.
evidence: The fossil record of the group begins with pollen, which is abundant and diagnostic, and only later with flowers themselves — Archaefructus from the Yixian beds being among the earliest reasonably complete. Molecular clocks consistently place the origin tens of millions of years before the oldest fossils, and reconciling those two lines is exactly the part that remains unresolved.

title: The Jehol Biota
detail: Volcanic ash falls repeatedly over a lake system in Liaoning and buries everything in it. The result is the richest window on Cretaceous land life anywhere: feathered dinosaurs, early birds, mammals with their fur and stomach contents, insects, flowers. Sinosauropteryx, described in 1996, was the first non-avian dinosaur found with feathers, and it settled the bird question for almost everyone who had been holding out.
evidence: Ash falls give two things at once — instantaneous burial, which preserves soft tissue, and datable minerals, which fix the age to within a few hundred thousand years. The commercial fossil trade around these beds has also produced forgeries, including a composite that was published as a missing link in 1999 and exposed within months, so provenance is checked far more carefully here than at most sites.

title: Ocean Anoxic Event 2
detail: Volcanic activity floods the atmosphere with carbon dioxide, the sea warms and stratifies, plankton bloom on the nutrients and their decay strips the oxygen from the water below. Black organic mud accumulates across the world's shelves and basins for a few hundred thousand years. A large share of the world's oil is that mud — the events that nearly suffocated the Cretaceous ocean are the reason there is petroleum to extract.
evidence: The same black horizon is correlated between continents by carbon isotope excursion and by microfossil zones, which is what shows it is one global event. Trace-metal depletion and iron speciation confirm oxygen-free bottom water; osmium isotopes point to a volcanic trigger by identifying a pulse of mantle-derived material entering the ocean.
facts: Source rock for much of the world's oil

title: The Chalk
detail: Warm shallow seas over Europe fill with coccolithophores, and their plates settle to make a white ooze that becomes hundreds of metres of chalk. The White Cliffs of Dover are that ooze. A cubic centimetre of chalk contains on the order of a thousand million individual plates, each from a single-celled alga, and the whole formation was laid down at something like a few centimetres per thousand years.
evidence: Put chalk under an electron microscope and the plates are visible individually and identifiable to species — the rock is not chalk-like, it is made of them. Deposition rate is calculated from the thickness of the formation divided by the duration its microfossil zones represent. The flint bands running through it are silica from sponges, redistributed after burial.

title: The Western Interior Seaway
detail: A shallow sea a thousand kilometres wide runs from the Arctic to the Gulf of Mexico, splitting North America into two land masses for tens of millions of years. It is warm, and it is full: giant fish, long-necked plesiosaurs, mosasaurs up to fifteen metres, ammonites, and above them pterosaurs with wingspans wider than a small aircraft. Kansas and Nebraska were, for a long time, deep water.
evidence: Mapped from the marine sediments themselves, which cover the interior of the continent and pinch out along its former shorelines — those shorelines can be traced on a map. The Smoky Hill Chalk of Kansas is one of the richest marine vertebrate deposits anywhere, and much of the American Museum's early collection came out of it.

title: Tyrannosaurus
detail: Twelve metres, around eight tonnes, and a skull built as a bone-crushing tool — its bite is the most powerful yet calculated for any land animal. Its eyes face forward with substantial overlap, giving genuine depth perception, and the olfactory bulbs are enormous. It appears in the very last two million years of the Cretaceous; it is closer in time to us than it is to Stegosaurus.
evidence: Bite force is modelled from jaw muscle attachment areas and checked against the puncture marks it left in other animals' bones, which can be tested against the failure strength of bone. Age at death is read from growth rings in the limb bones — the same principle as tree rings — which show it reached full size in about two decades and rarely lived past thirty.

title: The Deccan Traps
detail: One of the largest volcanic provinces of the last quarter-billion years erupts across western India, laying down lava kilometres thick over a few hundred thousand years either side of the boundary. It was pumping carbon dioxide and sulfur into the atmosphere before the asteroid arrived and continued afterwards. Whether it weakened the world first, or merely coincided, is the live argument in the field.
evidence: Dated by argon and by uranium–lead on individual flows, which now bracket the eruption tightly enough to show it straddles the boundary rather than sitting neatly before it. Climate effects are read from temperature proxies in marine sections, which record warming pulses in the run-up. The dispute is not about whether it happened but about how much of the extinction it can account for.

title: Chicxulub
detail: An object around ten kilometres across strikes the Yucatán at a steep angle, into shallow water over sulfur-rich rock — close to the worst possible target. It excavates a crater a hundred and eighty kilometres wide, throws molten rock across the planet, and injects enough sulfate aerosol into the stratosphere to shut down photosynthesis for years. The Alvarez team proposed it in 1980 from a thin layer of iridium; the crater itself was not identified until 1991, in oil company survey data that had been sitting unexamined.
evidence: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust and common in asteroids, and the boundary layer is enriched with it worldwide. Alongside it are shocked quartz grains, which form only at pressures achievable by impact or nuclear detonation, and glass spherules that get larger the closer you sample to the Gulf of Mexico — a gradient pointing straight at the crater. At Tanis in North Dakota, a deposit appears to record the seiche waves that arrived within an hour.

title: The End-Cretaceous Extinction
detail: Around three quarters of species disappear, including every dinosaur that was not a bird, all the pterosaurs, the ammonites, the mosasaurs and the plesiosaurs. Body size is the clearest filter: essentially nothing over about twenty-five kilograms on land survives. What comes through are small things that could burrow, shelter, eat detritus and wait — which is to say birds, and mammals, and the ancestors of nearly everything now alive on land.
evidence: The pattern is counted from occurrence data spanning the boundary, and the size filter is the most robust part of it. Working out whether the dinosaurs were already declining beforehand is genuinely hard, because the number of fossil-bearing sites of latest Cretaceous age is small and shrinking sample size mimics real decline. The current weight of evidence is that they were not in serious trouble until the impact.
facts: Almost nothing over ≈25 kg on land

title: The Paleogene Opens
detail: A quiet, emptied world that is about to get very warm. Nothing on land is bigger than a badger. The forests come back within a few thousand years and spread until they reach both poles — palms grow in Wyoming, crocodile relatives live on Ellesmere Island inside the Arctic Circle, and Antarctica is covered in temperate rainforest. There is no ice anywhere on the planet. Into the ecological space the dinosaurs left, mammals expand from small nocturnal insectivores into everything: within ten million years there are large browsers, hoofed runners and the first primates.
evidence: The absence of ice is read from oxygen isotopes in seafloor foraminifera, which give a continuous temperature curve for the last sixty-six million years and show this as one of the warmest stretches in it. The polar forests are excavated rather than inferred, from fossil wood and leaf beds in Arctic Canada and Antarctica. The mammal radiation is counted from body-size distributions in successive faunas, which shift upward remarkably fast after the boundary.
facts: Nothing larger than a badger, at first

title: The Fern Spike
detail: In the centimetres of rock directly above the impact layer, the pollen of flowering plants nearly vanishes and is replaced by an overwhelming abundance of fern spores. Ferns are the first thing back after a forest is destroyed — they colonise bare ground from wind-blown spores and need no soil to speak of. The spike lasts perhaps a thousand years, and then the forest returns. It is the fossil record of a planet-wide recovery from a burn.
evidence: Counted from palynology: pollen and spores are extracted from the rock by acid digestion and identified under a microscope, giving proportions rather than presences. The same inversion is found in North America, Japan and New Zealand at the same horizon. The modern analogue is direct — the identical spike is measured after volcanic eruptions and forest fires today.

title: The PETM
detail: Something releases an enormous quantity of carbon into the atmosphere and the world warms by five to eight degrees in perhaps twenty thousand years. The deep ocean acidifies until the carbonate on the seafloor dissolves, leaving a band of red clay where there should be white ooze. Mammals respond by shrinking — horses drop by about a third. It took the planet nearly two hundred thousand years to draw that carbon back down, and it is the closest natural analogue we have to what is being done now, at roughly a tenth of the current rate.
evidence: The carbon is identified by its isotopes: a sharp global drop in carbon-13 that requires a source depleted in it, which points at organic carbon rather than volcanic. Acidification is visible physically in ocean cores as the carbonate compensation depth shoals and dissolves the seafloor. The dwarfing is measured from tooth size in successive mammal populations through the interval.

title: The First Primates
detail: Small, nocturnal, arboreal animals with grasping hands, nails instead of claws, and eyes rotated to the front of the skull. Forward-facing eyes cost you a wide field of view and buy you overlapping vision — the ability to judge distance precisely, which is what you need to jump between branches. Teilhardina appears across North America, Europe and Asia within about twenty-five thousand years of the warming, spreading through forests that had just reached the Arctic.
evidence: Primate status is read from the skeleton — an opposable big toe, nails, and the bony bar enclosing the eye socket. The dispersal timing comes from tying specimens on three continents to the same carbon isotope excursion, which acts as a single global marker horizon far more precise than any fossil correlation could be.

title: India Meets Asia
detail: India, which has been crossing an ocean alone for tens of millions of years, arrives. There is no ocean floor left to subduct, so the two continents crumple, and the crust ends up doubled in thickness. The Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau are the result, and they are still rising. They also start a monsoon, and expose a colossal area of fresh silicate rock to tropical rain — which consumes carbon dioxide, and helps cool the planet for the rest of the era.
evidence: The collision is dated from the youngest marine sediments trapped in the suture zone, which give the moment the sea between them closed. Uplift history is read from the cooling ages of minerals as they are exhumed, and from the sediment volume delivered to the Bengal Fan. The weathering effect is tracked by strontium isotopes in seawater, which shift as Himalayan material reaches the ocean.

title: Whales Go Back
detail: A lineage of hoofed land mammals returns to the water over about ten million years, and the sequence is preserved almost step by step: Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal at the water's edge with whale ears; Ambulocetus, an otter-like swimmer; Rodhocetus, with shortened legs; Basilosaurus, fully aquatic and eighteen metres long, still carrying hind limbs the size of a hand. Molecular work said whales were closest to hippos, which palaeontologists resisted — until fossil ankles settled it.
evidence: The clinching evidence is a single bone. Artiodactyls have a distinctive double-pulley ankle bone found in no other group; when complete hind limbs of early whales were recovered in Pakistan in 2001, they had exactly that ankle. Two independent lines — gene sequences from living animals and a bone from a fifty-million-year-old fossil — converged on the same unexpected answer.

title: The Azolla Event
detail: The Arctic Ocean is nearly landlocked and its surface goes fresh, and a floating fern colonises it. Azolla doubles its mass every few days, and it does this across an area the size of a continent, for perhaps eight hundred thousand years. The mats die, sink into water with no oxygen, and are buried instead of rotting. The amount of carbon this removed from the atmosphere may have been enough to help tip the world out of its greenhouse state.
evidence: Found in 2004 in cores drilled from the Lomonosov Ridge, which recovered metres of sediment made largely of Azolla remains — freshwater plant material at the bottom of what is now the Arctic Ocean. That it grew there rather than washing in is shown by intact reproductive structures. How much carbon it actually removed remains an estimate, and a contested one.

title: The Messel Pit
detail: A flooded volcanic crater in Germany with stagnant, poisoned bottom water, into which animals fell and never decayed. The oil shale preserves fur, feathers, skin outlines, stomach contents and the structural colour of beetles, still iridescent. There are bats with the remains of their last meal inside them, and a horse that died pregnant with the foal still in place. It was very nearly turned into a landfill in the 1970s.
evidence: Soft tissue here survives as bacterial films that replicated the original outline as the body decomposed — so what is preserved is a microbial cast rather than the tissue itself, which is why the outlines are sharp but the interiors are not. Beetle colour is structural rather than pigmented, produced by microscopic layering in the cuticle that survives intact and still refracts light.

title: Antarctica Freezes
detail: South America and Australia finish separating from Antarctica, and for the first time water can flow all the way around the continent without meeting land. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current establishes itself, cutting Antarctica off from warm water arriving from the north, and the continent glaciates in geologically almost no time. The world flips from greenhouse to icehouse, and has stayed there. The rainforests of Antarctica die and are buried under the ice they are still beneath.
evidence: The oxygen isotope curve from seafloor cores shows an abrupt step at this boundary — one of the sharpest features in the entire sixty-six-million-year record. The gateway openings are dated from the seafloor magnetic record of each, and ice-rafted debris appears in Southern Ocean sediments at the same time, which requires glaciers reaching the sea.

title: The Neogene Opens
detail: Cooler, drier, and increasingly seasonal. Antarctica is under ice, the continents are close to where we would recognise them, and the closed forests that had covered the warm world are opening into woodland, savanna and eventually open grassland. That is a genuinely new kind of landscape: grass survives being eaten because it grows from the base rather than the tip, so for the first time there is a plant that rewards being grazed, and animals reorganise around it. The mammals of this world are the ones we would half recognise — horses, elephants, cats, apes.
evidence: The cooling is the same benthic isotope curve, which trends steadily downward through this interval. The spread of grassland is read from phytoliths, the microscopic silica bodies grasses make, which survive in soils and are identifiable to plant group; and from the wear patterns and crown height of herbivore teeth, which change as diets shift from leaves to grass.

title: The Age of Apes
detail: For a stretch of the Miocene there are more kinds of ape than monkey, spread from Spain to China, in the warm forests before the drying. Proconsul, Dryopithecus, Sivapithecus, Gigantopithecus — dozens of genera, in a range of body plans, most of which leave no descendants. What survives that contraction is a handful of lineages in Africa and Southeast Asia, and one of them is ours. Today there are hundreds of monkey species and a handful of apes; then it was the other way round.
evidence: Counted from named genera in the fossil record, with the usual caveat that ape teeth are distinctive and preserve well, which flatters the count. The contraction tracks the closing of the forest belt as the world dried, which is independently documented from plant and soil evidence across the same regions.

title: Megalodon
detail: The largest shark that has ever lived, with teeth the size of a hand — up to eighteen centimetres along the diagonal. Estimates of its length have ranged from fifteen to twenty-five metres and have been revised repeatedly, because almost nothing but the teeth and a few vertebrae survive. It hunted whales; there are whale bones with its bite marks on them, and nursery grounds have been identified from concentrations of small teeth.
evidence: Body size is extrapolated from tooth height using regressions built on living great whites, which is a long extrapolation from a much smaller animal and is why the numbers keep moving. A 2022 study using the vertebral column reached a different answer again. What is not in doubt is the diet: the bite marks on whale bone match the serration pattern of the teeth.

title: The Grasslands Take Over
detail: Between about eight and six million years ago, grasses using a different photosynthetic pathway spread across the tropics and subtropics of every continent almost simultaneously. Savanna replaces woodland over enormous areas. Grass carries silica, which wears teeth down, so grazers evolve teeth with tall crowns that keep erupting through life — and the horses, antelope and elephants of the modern world are shaped by this. So, in Africa, is an ape that comes down out of the trees.
evidence: This is one of the cleanest signals in the record. The two photosynthetic pathways fix carbon isotopes differently, and the animals that eat them lock that ratio into their tooth enamel, which survives essentially unaltered. Measuring enamel from dated fossils gives a direct diet history — and the shift shows up on four continents within the same two million years.

title: The Split
detail: A population of African apes divides, and the two halves stop interbreeding. One line leads to chimpanzees and bonobos; the other, through a long series of forms that are not us and are not chimps, leads here. There was no moment and no first human — just a slow separation, apparently with some interbreeding continuing for a while after it began. Sahelanthropus, from Chad, sits at about this depth and may be on our side of it, or near it.
evidence: The date comes from molecular clocks: counting the differences between human and chimpanzee genomes and dividing by a mutation rate measured directly in living families. Rate estimates have shifted, moving the date between about six and eight million years. The fossils are sparse and fragmentary, and whether Sahelanthropus walked upright is argued from the angle of the hole where the spine enters the skull, and from a femur described only in 2022.

title: The Mediterranean Dries Up
detail: The connection to the Atlantic closes, and a sea evaporates. Over several hundred thousand years the Mediterranean becomes a set of hypersaline lakes on a floor two or three kilometres below sea level, and lays down a salt deposit over a kilometre thick. Rivers cut gorges down to the new base level — the Nile carved a canyon below Cairo deeper than the Grand Canyon, now buried under sediment. Then the Atlantic breaks back through, and the basin refills, possibly in a couple of years.
evidence: Drilling in 1970 recovered evaporite minerals from the deep Mediterranean floor, which cannot form in open ocean. Seismic surveys map the salt layer's thickness and the buried river gorges beneath the modern deltas. The speed of the refill is estimated from the size of the erosional channel cut through the Gibraltar sill, which implies a discharge orders of magnitude beyond any river.

title: The Laetoli Footprints
detail: Ash falls from a volcano in Tanzania, rain dampens it, several hominins walk across, and the ash sets like cement. What is preserved is not bones but behaviour: a trail of upright footprints with a proper arch, a forward-driving big toe held in line with the others, and a heel-first stride. Whoever made them was walking as we walk, more than three million years ago, with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's. Bipedalism came first, long before the brain.
evidence: The prints themselves are the evidence, and they are unusually direct — foot anatomy and gait are read from the impressions rather than reconstructed from a skeleton. The ash is dated radiometrically above and below. Lucy, from beds of similar age in Ethiopia, provides the matching skeleton: a hip and knee built for upright walking on an animal barely over a metre tall.
facts: Modern arch, stride and big toe

title: The First Stone Tools
detail: Somebody strikes one rock against another to make a sharp edge. The Lomekwi assemblage in Kenya is large, crude and older than any known member of our own genus, which would mean toolmaking began before Homo did. Sharp stone changes what an animal can eat — it opens up meat and marrow that no hominin body could otherwise process — and that dietary shift is one of the leading explanations for what paid for a larger brain.
evidence: The claim rests on the flakes being deliberately struck rather than naturally fractured, which is argued from the scar patterns, the striking platforms, and the fact that some cores and flakes can be fitted back together. It is contested; other researchers read the assemblage as accidental. The Oldowan tools from around 2.6 million years ago are not disputed by anyone.

title: The Great American Interchange
detail: The Isthmus of Panama closes and two continents that had been separate for tens of millions of years are joined. Animals cross in both directions, but not equally: North American groups — cats, bears, deer, camelids — move south and largely displace the native South American fauna, and most of the giant marsupial predators and strange hoofed mammals that had evolved there in isolation do not survive it. Only a handful go the other way and stay, among them the armadillo, the opossum and the porcupine.
evidence: Reconstructed from the appearance of each group in the fossil record on the far continent, dated bed by bed, which gives directions and rough timings. The asymmetry is measured by counting families that established themselves each way. The closure date itself has been challenged, with some geological evidence arguing for a much earlier connection, and the debate is not settled.

title: The Quaternary Opens
detail: Ice sheets begin forming in the northern hemisphere, and from here the world oscillates. At a glacial maximum, ice kilometres thick covers Canada and Scandinavia, sea level falls by around a hundred and twenty metres, Britain is a peninsula of Europe and you can walk from Siberia to Alaska. Across northern Eurasia stretches the mammoth steppe — cold, dry, productive grassland, the largest biome on Earth at the time, carrying mammoth, horse, bison and lion. Between glaciations the ice retreats and the forests come back. This is the world our own genus grows up in, and the instability may be the point.
evidence: The cycles are read from oxygen isotopes in seafloor cores, which record global ice volume continuously, and matched to the calculated wobbles of Earth's orbit. Sea-level fall is measured from drowned coral terraces and from the sediments of exposed continental shelves. Ice cores give the atmosphere itself, sampled directly, for the last eight hundred thousand years.

title: The Oldowan
detail: Simple, effective and undisputed: a cobble struck to detach flakes with edges sharp enough to cut hide and disarticulate a carcass. The same basic method is used essentially unchanged for over a million years, across Africa and then beyond it, which is a stretch of technological stasis difficult to imagine. Cut marks on animal bone from the same beds show what it was for.
evidence: Deliberate manufacture is demonstrated by refitting — flakes can be fitted back onto the cores they came from, reassembling the sequence of blows. Function is shown by cut marks on bone whose cross-section under a microscope matches stone rather than tooth, and by experimental butchery producing identical traces.

title: Homo erectus
detail: The first hominin with our body proportions — long legs, short arms, a narrow trunk, built for walking and running long distances in open country rather than climbing. It is the first to leave Africa, reaching Georgia by around 1.8 million years ago and Java soon after, and the first to make the Acheulean handaxe, a symmetrical teardrop biface that requires planning a shape before you start. It persisted for well over a million years, which is several times longer than our species has existed.
evidence: Body proportions are known from the Turkana Boy skeleton, unusually complete for a hominin. The dispersal dates come from radiometric ages on volcanic deposits at Dmanisi in Georgia and in Java. That handaxes were made to a mental template is argued from their consistency across huge distances and time spans, far beyond what raw material or function requires.

title: Fire
detail: Cooking makes food safer, softer and far easier to extract energy from, which lets an animal support a smaller gut and a larger brain. Fire also extends the day, deters predators, and creates the first reason to sit together in one place after dark. When control began is genuinely uncertain: there is burnt bone and ash deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa at around a million years, but unambiguous hearths only appear several hundred thousand years later.
evidence: The difficulty is distinguishing a fire that was made from one that merely happened. The strongest cases combine ash located where lightning and wind cannot reach, burning temperatures consistent with wood fires, repeated use of the same spot, and burnt material clustered rather than scattered. Wonderwerk has most of these; many earlier claims have not survived scrutiny.
facts: Smaller gut, more energy for the brain

title: The Ice Ages Change Rhythm
detail: For the first million and a half years of the Quaternary, glaciations come and go every forty-one thousand years, following the tilt of Earth's axis. Then, without any corresponding change in the orbit, the rhythm slows to roughly a hundred thousand years and the swings become far larger — long slow build-ups of ice ending in abrupt collapses. The orbital forcing did not change; the planet's response to it did, and why is still not agreed.
evidence: The change is unmistakable in the stacked oxygen isotope records from dozens of ocean cores, which is what makes it a puzzle rather than a measurement error: the astronomical driver is calculable and demonstrably unchanged. Explanations invoke the gradual removal of soft sediment from beneath the northern ice sheets, or a slow decline in carbon dioxide crossing a threshold, and the record cannot yet distinguish them.

title: The Ice Cores
detail: Snow falling on Antarctica never melts. It compacts into ice, sealing bubbles of air as it goes, and those bubbles are samples of the actual atmosphere on the day they closed. Drilling down through three kilometres of it recovers a continuous record back eight hundred thousand years — temperature, carbon dioxide, methane, dust, volcanic ash, all read layer by layer. It is the only archive of the deep past that is not a proxy for the thing you want to know but the thing itself.
evidence: Age comes from counting annual layers where they can be resolved, and from ice-flow models and matched volcanic markers deeper down. Gas concentrations are measured by crushing the ice under vacuum and analysing what comes out. Temperature is read from the isotopic composition of the ice itself. Blue-ice sites in Antarctica have since yielded fragments over two million years old.

title: The Mammoth Steppe
detail: At glacial maxima, a single continuous grassland runs from Spain across Eurasia, over the exposed Bering land bridge, and into Canada — the most extensive biome on the planet. It is cold and very dry, and it is productive: dense enough in grass and herbs to support mammoth, woolly rhino, horse, bison, saiga and the lions and hyenas that followed them. Nothing like it exists today, and its disappearance at the end of the last glaciation took most of its large animals with it.
evidence: Reconstructed from pollen and from plant DNA recovered directly from permafrost, which shows a herb-rich grassland rather than the mossy tundra that replaced it. Animal densities are inferred from bone accumulations and from the isotopic composition of their remains. Frozen carcasses in Siberian and Alaskan permafrost preserve stomach contents, giving diet directly.

title: The Neanderthals
detail: A separate human lineage, adapted to glacial Europe and western Asia: heavier built, larger nosed, with brains averaging slightly larger than ours. They made tools, used fire, buried their dead, cared for the injured, and made pigment and ornament. They were not a failed draft of us — they were a parallel one, and they lasted several hundred thousand years. The Sima de los Huesos in Spain, at around 430,000 years, has yielded the oldest hominin nuclear DNA recovered.
evidence: Their relationship to us is not read from bones but sequenced: the Neanderthal genome was published in 2010, from powdered bone, and showed that non-African humans today carry a small percentage of Neanderthal ancestry. That result had been proposed and rejected on morphological grounds for a century, and was settled in a laboratory rather than a museum drawer.
facts: Slightly larger than ours on average

title: Jebel Irhoud
detail: The oldest fossils assigned to our own species, from a collapsed cave in Morocco — five thousand kilometres from East Africa, where everyone had been looking. The faces are essentially modern; the braincases are not, being long and low rather than globular. Whatever we are, we did not arrive all at once, and we did not arrive in one place.
evidence: Re-dated in 2017 by thermoluminescence on flints burnt in the same layer, which measures how long ago a stone was heated. The result moved the site from around 160,000 years to around 315,000 and roughly doubled the age of the species. Facial anatomy is compared landmark by landmark against modern and archaic skulls rather than judged by eye.

title: Misliya Cave
detail: An upper jaw with teeth, found on Mount Carmel, and the earliest evidence of our species outside Africa by a wide margin. It shows that people were leaving far earlier than the successful dispersal that peopled the rest of the world — and that most of those earlier attempts went nowhere.
evidence: Three independent dating methods were run on the specimen and its layer — uranium series, electron spin resonance and thermoluminescence — and agreed on 177,000 to 194,000 years. Species assignment rests on dental features, which are diagnostic but a smaller sample of anatomy than a skull would give.

title: Denisova Cave
detail: An entire human population identified from a fingertip. The bone was too fragmentary to classify by shape, so it was sequenced instead, and the genome belonged to neither us nor Neanderthals but to a third lineage nobody had suspected. Denisovan ancestry survives today at its highest levels in New Guinea and Australia, thousands of kilometres from the only cave that has yielded good remains.
evidence: This is a group defined by DNA before it was defined by anatomy, which had never happened before. The cave has since produced a bone fragment from a girl whose mother was Neanderthal and whose father was Denisovan — a first-generation hybrid, found by screening thousands of scraps for collagen fingerprints and then sequencing the hits.

title: Toba
detail: The largest volcanic eruption of the last two million years. It threw out around two thousand eight hundred cubic kilometres of material and left a caldera a hundred kilometres long, now a lake. It was once argued that the resulting volcanic winter nearly exterminated our species, reducing us to a few thousand individuals — a story that has not held up well.
evidence: The ash is found as a distinct layer across India, the Indian Ocean and East Africa, which is what fixes both its size and its date. The bottleneck claim came from genetic diversity estimates and has since weakened: excavations in India and southern Africa show occupation continuing across the ash layer with no visible break.

title: Blombos Cave
detail: A piece of ochre with a cross-hatched pattern deliberately engraved into it, and elsewhere in the same cave a shell containing a prepared ochre-and-fat pigment mixture with the tools still beside it. The engraving means nothing that can be recovered. What it demonstrates is that someone made a mark that was not for use — the earliest firm evidence of that habit anywhere.
evidence: Deliberate engraving is established by the regularity of the lines and by their sequence, which can be read from how they cross one another. The pigment workshop is dated by optically stimulated luminescence on the surrounding sand, which measures when quartz grains were last exposed to daylight.

title: The Crossing to Sahul
detail: Australia and New Guinea were joined, but never connected to Asia — even at the lowest sea level there were open water crossings of tens of kilometres. Getting there required watercraft and the intention to use them, which makes this the earliest evidence of deliberate sea voyaging anywhere. Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land holds ground-edge axes and processed ochre from around sixty-five thousand years ago.
evidence: Dated by optically stimulated luminescence on individual sand grains, which also tests whether the deposit has been disturbed — if grains of very different ages sit together, the layer has been mixed. The 2017 result of 65,000 years is contested by researchers who argue for exactly that kind of mixing, and the debate is unresolved.

title: Homo naledi
detail: A hominin with a brain a third the size of ours, hands built for climbing and feet built for walking, found deep inside a cave system reachable only through a chute eighteen centimetres wide. Fifteen individuals, no predator damage, no sediment washed in with them. The excavators argue they were carried there deliberately — which would put mortuary behaviour in a small-brained species, at a time when our own were already alive on the same continent.
evidence: The species is described from over 1,500 bone fragments, the richest hominin assemblage in Africa. The date came later and was the surprise: 335,000 to 236,000 years, from uranium series and electron spin resonance on teeth, placing it far more recently than its anatomy suggested. The deliberate-disposal argument rests on taphonomy — how the bones got there — and remains actively disputed.

title: Omo Kibish
detail: Two partial skulls found by Richard Leakey's team in 1967 and long argued over. Omo I has the rounded braincase and small face that Jebel Irhoud lacks — anatomically it is us. What kept moving was the date, and each revision pushed it further back.
evidence: The site sits below a thick volcanic ash. In 2022 that ash was chemically fingerprinted and matched to a dated eruption of the Shala volcano, three hundred kilometres away, giving a firm minimum of 233,000 years. Because the ash lies above the fossils, the bones can only be older — a rare case where the geology gives a hard floor rather than an estimate.
facts: Ash matched to a distant eruption

title: Pinnacle Point
detail: Caves in a sea cliff holding the earliest firm evidence of people eating shellfish, along with ground ochre and stone blades made from silcrete that had been heated in a fire to make it easier to work. Cooking rock to improve it is a two-stage process with a delayed payoff, which is a particular kind of thinking. The date coincides with a long glacial period when much of Africa was arid — and the coast was one of the few reliable larders left.
evidence: Shellfish are identified from the species present in the deposit, brought from the shore rather than washed in. Heat treatment is demonstrated experimentally: silcrete heated to around 300°C changes its fracture behaviour and gains a distinctive gloss on surfaces broken afterwards, and both the gloss and the archaeomagnetic signature of heating are present.

title: Herto
detail: Three skulls from the Afar depression, anatomically modern but robust enough to be given their own subspecies. All three carry cut marks and one is polished from repeated handling — defleshed after death and then kept, over a long enough period to wear the bone smooth. It is not a burial. Whatever it was, someone was doing something with the dead that involved returning to them.
evidence: Dated by argon–argon on the volcanic layers bracketing the sediments, to between 160,000 and 154,000 years. The cut marks are distinguished from carnivore damage under a microscope by their cross-section — stone leaves a V-shaped groove, teeth do not. The polish is compared against experimentally handled bone.

title: The Oldest Beads
detail: Thirty-three sea snail shells, each pierced in the same place and worn smooth where a cord ran through. A bead does nothing. It carries no information about the world, catches no food and cuts nothing — it exists to be seen by someone else, which means it is a message, and a message requires a shared code. These are the oldest objects known to have been made for that purpose.
evidence: The perforations are argued to be deliberate rather than natural predation by their consistent position and by wear traces on the hole edges, matched against experimentally strung replicas. Ochre residue survives on some. The date, 142,000 to 150,000 years, comes from uranium series on the surrounding deposits.

title: Qafzeh
detail: Modern humans buried in a cave in the Levant, some with objects placed with them — a young person laid with the antlers of a red deer held across the chest. There is ochre, and shells brought from the Mediterranean, and evidence of fires used to heat them. This is a hundred thousand years before the successful dispersal out of Africa, and this population left no descendants anywhere.
evidence: Thermoluminescence on burnt flints from the burial layers gives 92,000 to 115,000 years. Deliberate burial is inferred from body position, from grave cuts visible in the sediment, and from articulation — a body that decays where it fell scatters, and these did not.

title: The Katanda Harpoons
detail: Barbed points carved from bone, finely made, found with the remains of very large catfish. Complex bone technology of this kind was thought to be a European invention of the Upper Palaeolithic, some fifty thousand years later. The dates were disbelieved for years for exactly that reason, and the site is one of the clearest cases of a chronology being resisted because of where it was rather than what it showed.
evidence: Dated by electron spin resonance and optically stimulated luminescence on the enclosing sands, giving around 90,000 years, later supported by a second round of dating. That the points are worked rather than naturally shaped is clear from the carved barbs, which have no natural analogue.

title: Panga ya Saidi
detail: A cave occupied more or less continuously for seventy-eight thousand years — the longest unbroken sequence in East Africa. It sits in coastal forest rather than the savanna or the shore, which undercuts the tidy story that our expansion was driven by any single habitat. The layers hold ostrich eggshell beads, a carved bone tool, worked ochre, and later a human burial.
evidence: The value here is stratigraphic: one place, one column of sediment, sampled continuously and dated at many levels by optically stimulated luminescence and radiocarbon. That makes changes in behaviour readable as change over time rather than as differences between sites, which is the usual and much weaker comparison.

title: The Oldest Bedding
detail: Compacted layers of sedge and rush, brought in and spread on the cave floor to sleep on, and laid over with the crushed leaves of a tree whose foliage kills mosquitoes and other biting insects. The bedding was periodically burnt and fresh material laid down on the ash. Someone worked out that a particular plant repelled the things that bit you at night, and used it.
evidence: The plant species are identified from preserved cellular structure in the compressed layers, and one of them, Cryptocarya woodii, is chemically active against insects — a property tested in the laboratory rather than assumed. Burning is read from ash lenses interleaved with the bedding, showing repeated cleaning.

title: Did Neanderthals Paint?
detail: Red pigment on cave walls in three widely separated Spanish caves — a ladder-like shape, hand stencils, curtains of stalactite washed with colour. If the dates hold, the paint went on twenty thousand years before our species reached western Europe, which leaves only one candidate. It would mean the capacity for symbolic marking was not ours alone, and did not arrive with us.
evidence: Dated indirectly by uranium series on the thin carbonate crusts that grew over the pigment, giving a minimum age of about 64,800 years. The method is the weak point and the argument is live: critics contend the crusts can incorporate older uranium or lose it over time, and that open-system behaviour could inflate the ages.

title: Homo floresiensis
detail: An adult hominin a little over a metre tall with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's, on an island east of the Wallace Line that can only be reached across open water. Islands do this to large mammals — Flores also had dwarf elephants — but a dwarfed human was not on anyone's list. They made stone tools, and they were still there when our own species was in the region.
evidence: The pathological-modern-human explanation, offered repeatedly since 2004, has not survived: the wrist bones, shoulder and feet are primitive in ways no known disorder produces, and there is more than one individual. Revised stratigraphy in 2016 moved the youngest remains from 12,000 back to about 50,000 years, removing the overlap with farming populations that had made the story stranger still.

title: The Interbreeding
detail: Populations moving out of Africa meet Neanderthals and have children with them. Everyone alive today whose ancestry lies outside sub-Saharan Africa carries roughly one to two percent Neanderthal DNA as a result. Some of it was useful — variants affecting immunity and skin — and some was not: Neanderthal versions of certain genes were selected away within a few thousand generations.
evidence: Read from the length of Neanderthal segments in modern genomes. Recombination chops inherited blocks shorter every generation, so segment length is a clock, and it dates the main pulse to roughly 47,000 years ago. The 45,000-year-old Ust'-Ishim individual carries much longer blocks than anyone living, which independently confirms the mechanism.

title: Into Europe
detail: Teeth and bone fragments in a Bulgarian cave, with stone tools and pierced animal-tooth pendants — the earliest known modern humans in Europe, arriving while Neanderthals still held most of the continent. The two overlapped for several thousand years, and the pendants at this site are made in a style Neanderthals elsewhere were also producing, which raises the question of who was copying whom.
evidence: Most of the material is unidentifiable scrap, so the humans were found by ZooMS — mass spectrometry of collagen, which distinguishes species from a fragment too small to recognise by eye. Promising pieces were then sequenced. Radiocarbon on the same bones gives 45,900 to 42,600 years.

title: Ust'-Ishim Man
detail: A single thigh bone eroding out of a riverbank in Siberia, found by a carver looking for mammoth ivory. It yielded one of the oldest high-quality modern human genomes, and it turned out to be far more useful than its owner's story: because his Neanderthal ancestry sat in much longer unbroken blocks than anyone alive carries, he provided the calibration that dates the interbreeding itself.
evidence: Radiocarbon dates the bone to about 45,000 years. The genome was sequenced to high coverage from a sample with unusually good preservation, helped by permafrost. The dating logic is the strength here: segment length shortens at a known rate per generation, so a genome of known age converts that length into an absolute date for the admixture.

title: The Oldest Instrument
detail: A flute cut from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, twenty-two centimetres long, with five finger holes and a V-shaped notch carved into the blowing end. Replicas play a usable scale. Others from the same caves were made from mammoth ivory, which means splitting a tusk lengthways, hollowing both halves and sealing them back together airtight — a far harder object to make than a bird bone, and someone chose to.
evidence: Radiocarbon on associated material gives at least 40,000 years. The finger holes are demonstrably deliberate: they are spaced, sized and bevelled, with fine cut marks around them where the maker marked positions before boring. Playable reconstructions confirm the spacing produces a coherent scale rather than arbitrary pitches.

title: The Neanderthals End
detail: The last Neanderthal populations disappear, and the caves of the Rock of Gibraltar hold some of the youngest evidence of them anywhere. There is no single cause on offer that survives scrutiny — not violence, not intelligence, not a sudden climate event. What the record shows is small, scattered populations with low genetic diversity, absorbed and outnumbered over a few thousand years. They did not vanish entirely; part of them is in most of us.
evidence: Dating this is unusually hard, because a fraction of a percent of modern carbon contamination makes a 40,000-year-old sample look thousands of years younger. Re-dating European sites with improved purification pulled almost every late date backwards, and several claimed survivals to 28,000 years did not survive that scrutiny.

title: The Sungir Burials
detail: Two children buried head to head, covered in some ten thousand beads carved from mammoth ivory, with spears made from straightened mammoth tusks — a process nobody has fully worked out. Each bead takes roughly an hour to make. The labour represented by these graves is on the order of several years of one person's work, spent on two children, in a landscape at the edge of the ice.
evidence: Bead counts come from excavation records; the manufacturing time is an experimental estimate from replication. The pair were long assumed to be brothers; genome sequencing in 2017 showed they were no closer than second cousins, and that the wider Sungir group deliberately avoided close-kin pairings — which implies a social network extending well beyond the camp.
facts: Years of work, for two children

title: Above the Arctic Circle
detail: People living at seventy degrees north in the middle of an ice age, hunting mammoth, bison and woolly rhino, and making beads and needles. Needles matter more than they sound: tailored, fitted clothing is the only way a tropical animal survives an Arctic winter, and it is the technology that opens the far north — and, eventually, the route into the Americas.
evidence: Radiocarbon on bone and ivory from the occupation layers gives about 32,000 years. Two individuals from the site were sequenced in 2019 and belong to a population that contributed to later Native American ancestry, tying the Arctic occupation to the peopling of the Americas rather than leaving it an isolated curiosity.

title: Pottery Before Farming
detail: Fragments of fired clay pots from a cave in southern China, made by hunter-gatherers at the coldest point of the last ice age — ten thousand years before anyone farmed anything. The standard sequence has agriculture produce settlement and settlement produce pottery. Here the pots come first, made by mobile people, apparently for cooking shellfish and boiling bones for fat.
evidence: Dated by radiocarbon on bone and charcoal from the layers holding the sherds, with the stratigraphy checked closely because a cave floor can be disturbed. Soot on the outer surfaces and scorching patterns indicate use over fire rather than storage. Similar early dates have since come from Japan and the Russian Far East.

title: Lascaux
detail: Nearly two thousand figures — horses, aurochs, stags, one bear — painted and engraved across a cave found by four teenagers following a dog down a hole in 1940. The animals are drawn with an understanding of movement and foreshortening that no one taught anyone. It was opened to tourists, and the carbon dioxide and lamps of twelve hundred visitors a day grew algae and crystals on the walls; it was closed in 1963 and people now visit a replica.
evidence: Dated by radiocarbon on charcoal and on organic material in the pigments, and by the animals depicted, which match the local ice-age fauna. The conservation history is itself evidence of something: the paintings survived seventeen thousand years sealed, and fifteen years of visitors nearly destroyed them.

title: The Dog
detail: A young dog buried with a man and a woman, in a grave with ochre and worked bone. Its teeth show it survived a severe bout of distemper as a puppy — an illness that would have killed it without weeks of someone keeping it warm, watered and fed. It could not have worked or hunted while sick. Somebody looked after it because they wanted to.
evidence: Radiocarbon dates the burial to about 14,200 years. The distemper diagnosis is read from enamel hypoplasia — bands of disrupted tooth growth that record the timing and duration of severe illness — and the pattern indicates at least two, probably three separate episodes, each weeks long.

title: The Clovis Point
detail: A fluted stone point, thinned by a channel struck from the base so it could be hafted to a shaft, found across North America within a few centuries. For most of the twentieth century it was taken to mark the arrival of the first Americans, and the model was defended so firmly that older claims were treated as errors by default. Monte Verde ended that, but the points remain one of the fastest technological spreads in the record.
evidence: The flute is the diagnostic feature and it is technically demanding — a large proportion of points break during the final strike, and knapping experiments show the failure rate is high enough that the design must have been maintained for reasons beyond pure efficiency. Distribution is mapped from thousands of finds; the tight date range comes from radiocarbon at the few sites with stratified organics.

title: The Tower of Jericho
detail: A stone tower eight and a half metres high with an internal staircase of twenty-two steps, built into a wall around a settlement of a few hundred people who had only just begun to farm. It is the oldest monumental structure known. What it was for is unresolved: a defence against nobody in particular, a flood barrier, or — from the alignment of its shadow at the summer solstice — something to do with marking time and with whoever controlled that knowledge.
evidence: Radiocarbon on organic material in the mudbrick and fill gives around 11,500 years. The defensive reading has weakened because no contemporary threat is evident and the wall does not enclose the settlement fully; the flood and solstice arguments both come from modelling the local topography and sightlines.

title: The First Herds
detail: Goats and sheep in the Zagros stop being hunted and start being managed. The archaeological signal is a change in who dies: hunters take adults of both sexes, herders kill young males and keep females alive to breed. Within a few generations the animals themselves change — smaller, with different horns — because the docile ones are the ones that survive to reproduce.
evidence: Read from culling profiles: the age and sex distribution of the bones in a deposit, reconstructed from tooth eruption and bone fusion. A shift toward young males is the signature of management, and it appears in the record before any change in the animals' anatomy — which means the practice is visible before its effects are.

title: Kuk Swamp
detail: Drainage ditches, mounds and planting holes dug into a highland wetland to grow taro, yam and banana — agriculture invented here independently, with no contact with the Fertile Crescent or China. It is one of a small number of places where farming was worked out from scratch, and for a long time it was left out of the story because the crops do not leave grains.
evidence: The field systems are excavated directly, with successive phases of ditching visible in the sediment and dated by radiocarbon. The crops themselves are identified from starch grains and phytoliths recovered from stone tools and soil, since roots and bananas leave nothing that survives as a seed — which is exactly why this region's agriculture was overlooked.

title: The First American Crop
detail: Squash seeds and rind from a dry rockshelter in Oaxaca, larger and thicker-walled than their wild ancestors — the earliest domesticated plant in the Americas, some two thousand years before maize. The shelter was used seasonally by a handful of people, which makes the point that domestication did not require settling down first.
evidence: Dated by accelerator radiocarbon directly on the seeds and rind, rather than on charcoal from the same layer, which removes any question of the plant material being intrusive. Domestication is identified from measurable changes — seed length, rind thickness, stem attachment — against a large sample of modern wild and cultivated squash.

title: Çatalhöyük
detail: Several thousand people living in mudbrick houses packed together with no streets between them — you walked across the roofs and climbed down a ladder into your home.
