title: The Battery
detail: Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch and concluded animals carry their own electricity. Volta disagreed, argued the effect came from the two different metals touching, and built a stack of zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked cloth to prove it. He was right, and the argument produced the first source of steady current — the thing electrical science had been missing.
evidence: The pile settled the dispute by producing the same effect with no animal present at all. Within weeks of Volta's letter being read in London, Nicholson and Carlisle used a pile to split water into hydrogen and oxygen — chemistry done with electricity, six weeks after the tool existed.

title: Humboldt
detail: Climbing a volcano with barometers and thermometers, he notices that the plants change with altitude in the same sequence they change with latitude, and draws it — a mountain in cross-section with vegetation bands labelled. Nature, he argued, is a single connected web, and he was the first to describe human-caused climate change, from deforestation around a Venezuelan lake.
evidence: His figure of Chimborazo is one of the first information graphics: measurements of temperature, pressure, humidity and species plotted against height on one image. The deforestation observation was made by measuring the lake's falling level and connecting it to clearance in the watershed — a causal claim supported by field data in 1800.
facts: One of the first data graphics

title: Atomic Theory
detail: Democritus guessed at atoms; Dalton made them quantitative. Elements combine in fixed whole-number ratios by weight, which is what you expect if each element consists of identical particles of a characteristic mass that join in small whole numbers. He published a table of relative atomic weights. It was the first version of atomism that could be checked by weighing things.
evidence: The law of multiple proportions is the key: when two elements form more than one compound, the weights of one that combine with a fixed weight of the other stand in simple ratios like 1:2. That pattern has no natural explanation unless matter is particulate, and it comes straight from the balance.

title: The Haitian Revolution
detail: Enslaved people in France's richest colony rise, defeat the colonial planters, then a British expedition, then a Spanish one, then a French army sent by Napoleon, and declare independence in 1804. It is the only successful large-scale slave revolt in history and the first state founded by formerly enslaved people. France then demanded reparations — for the loss of its slaves — and Haiti paid for 122 years.
evidence: The indemnity is documented in French treasury records: 150 million francs, later reduced, financed by French loans at punitive rates, with final payments made in 1947. A 2022 analysis of the transfers estimated the cost to Haiti in the tens of billions of present-day dollars, which is a large part of why the first free Black republic was kept poor.
facts: The freedom of its own people

title: Electromagnetism
detail: During a lecture, Ørsted notices that a compass needle near a wire swings when current flows — and that it sets itself at right angles to the wire rather than toward it, which is unlike any force then known. Electricity and magnetism are one phenomenon. Within months Ampère has the mathematics and within a decade there are motors.
evidence: The perpendicular deflection is what made it strange and important: every known force acted along the line between two bodies, and this one acted sideways, which is why it resisted explanation for decades until fields were invented. Ørsted checked carefully for artefacts before publishing, in Latin, to every scientific society in Europe at once.
facts: A compass deflecting near a current

title: Carnot
detail: A young engineer asks what limits the efficiency of a steam engine and finds the answer does not depend on the working substance or the cleverness of the design — only on the temperatures between which it runs. No engine can beat it. It is the second law of thermodynamics in embryo, written by a man of twenty-eight, using a theory of heat that was wrong.
evidence: He assumed heat was a conserved fluid, which it is not, and still got the limit right, because the conclusion depends on the impossibility of perpetual motion rather than on the nature of heat. The work was ignored for twenty-five years until Clapeyron restated it mathematically. Carnot died of cholera at 36 and his papers were burned as a precaution.
facts: A theory of heat that was false

title: Induction
detail: A bookbinder's apprentice with almost no formal education discovers that a changing magnetic field induces a current in a nearby wire — the principle of every generator and transformer since. Unable to follow the mathematics of his time, he thought instead in lines of force filling space, an idea his colleagues found naive and which turned out to be the field concept.
evidence: His laboratory notebooks are numbered paragraph by paragraph across forty years and survive complete, so the path of each discovery can be traced day by day, including the failures. Maxwell said explicitly that he had set out to translate Faraday's lines of force into mathematics, and that he found them rigorous where others had seen vagueness.

title: The Analytical Engine
detail: Babbage designs a mechanical computer with a store, a mill, conditional branching and punched-card input — a general-purpose machine, a century before one was built. Translating a paper about it, Ada Lovelace added notes three times longer than the original, including an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers and the observation that such a machine might work on anything representable by symbols, not only numbers.
evidence: The engine was never completed; Babbage kept redesigning it and the funding ran out. His Difference Engine No. 2 was built to his drawings by the Science Museum in 1991 and works to thirty-one digits, which shows the designs were sound and the Victorian machining adequate — the failure was organisational.
facts: It could manipulate symbols, not just numbers
From the original drawings — it works

title: Anaesthesia
detail: Before October 1846, surgery was done on conscious patients held down by assistants, and speed was the surgeon's principal virtue. Ether changed that in a single public demonstration, and within months it was in use across Europe. It made possible operations that could not previously be attempted because nobody could endure them.
evidence: The demonstration was public and witnessed, which is why the date is exact. The priority was then fought over for decades by four claimants, two of whom died in poverty and one by suicide. Nitrous oxide's anaesthetic property had been noted by Humphry Davy in 1800 and simply not pursued for forty-five years.

title: Semmelweis
detail: Two maternity clinics in the same hospital: one staffed by doctors, one by midwives. Women died of puerperal fever in the doctors' clinic at three or four times the rate. Semmelweis worked out that the doctors came straight from dissecting corpses, ordered handwashing in chlorinated lime, and the death rate fell to match. He had no germ theory to explain it, and he was dismissed.
evidence: He kept monthly mortality figures and published them, so the effect is visible as a step change in a time series — one of the earliest uses of hospital statistics to evaluate a practice. Colleagues rejected it partly because it implied they had been killing their patients. He died in an asylum in 1865, two years before Lister published on antisepsis.
facts: Germ theory did not yet exist

title: John Snow's Map
detail: During a cholera outbreak, Snow plots every death on a street map and finds them clustered around one water pump. The anomalies confirm it: a workhouse with its own well barely affected, a brewery whose workers drank beer untouched, and a widow who had the water carted to her in Hampstead and died there. He had the pump handle removed.
evidence: The map is the argument, and the outliers do the work — a cluster alone could reflect where people live, while a distant death traced to the same water source cannot. His larger study compared two water companies supplying interleaved houses on the same streets, one drawing from sewage-polluted Thames water, which is effectively a natural experiment.
facts: Plot deaths, look for the source
A natural experiment on water supply

title: Wallace
detail: Collecting specimens for sale in the Malay archipelago, and feverish with malaria, Wallace works out natural selection independently and posts it to Darwin, who had been sitting on the same idea for twenty years. He also noticed a sharp line through the islands where Asian fauna gives way to Australian, and correctly inferred deep water and long separation.
evidence: Wallace's Line is a genuine biogeographic boundary and was later explained by plate tectonics and the deep Lombok Strait, which stayed open even at glacial low sea level. The 1858 papers were read jointly at the Linnean Society; Wallace, who was in Asia and had not been consulted, accepted the arrangement and later titled his own book Darwinism.

title: On the Origin of Species
detail: More offspring are born than can survive; they vary; variation is heritable; therefore the variants that survive better become commoner. The argument is short and the book is long because Darwin knew what he was up against and spent four hundred pages answering objections before they were raised, including a chapter on the difficulties of his own theory.
evidence: He had no mechanism of inheritance — Mendel's work was published seven years later and went unread for thirty-five — so his account of how variation persisted was wrong in detail. The theory survived because the pattern it predicted kept turning up: in the fossil record, in biogeography, in embryology, and eventually in the genome.
facts: Short; the evidence is the book

title: Germ Theory
detail: Pasteur shows that fermentation and putrefaction are caused by living microorganisms carried in the air, not generated spontaneously from the matter itself. His swan-neck flask lets air in but traps dust in the bend; the broth stays sterile for years, and spoils within days once the neck is broken. Surgery, food preservation and public health all follow.
evidence: The flask is a beautifully designed control — the same broth, the same air, one variable. Several of his originals are still sterile in Paris after more than 150 years. His notebooks, opened to scholars in the 1970s, also show he was less scrupulous than his public accounts: the anthrax vaccine he demonstrated was prepared by a rival's method.
facts: Show the public story was tidied

title: Maxwell's Equations
detail: Four equations tie electricity and magnetism together, and they contain a surprise: they predict waves travelling at a speed computable from two constants measured in a laboratory. The number came out at the speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave, which nobody had expected, and there must be other wavelengths nobody had seen.
evidence: The prediction was confirmed when Hertz generated and detected radio waves in 1887, twenty-two years later and eight after Maxwell's death — a theory predicting an entire invisible spectrum before anyone had any way to look for it. Einstein said special relativity came out of thinking about what these equations imply.

title: Mendel
detail: A friar crosses pea plants for eight years, counting some twenty-eight thousand of them, and finds traits pass in discrete units that do not blend — a tall and a short parent give tall offspring, and shortness reappears in a quarter of the next generation. It is the answer to the problem that broke Darwin's account of inheritance, published seven years after the Origin and read by almost nobody for thirty-five.
evidence: His results are so close to the predicted ratios that Fisher argued in 1936 they were too good to be chance, and the dispute over whether he or an assistant tidied the counts has run ever since. The conclusions are correct regardless — they have been reproduced many times — which makes this a case of a right answer with suspicious arithmetic.

title: Antisepsis
detail: Reading Pasteur, Lister reasons that if wound infection is caused by organisms arriving from outside, then killing them at the wound should prevent it. He dresses wounds with carbolic acid and sprays it in the operating theatre. Mortality after amputation in his ward falls from around 45% to 15% in three years.
evidence: He published the before-and-after figures from his own ward, which is weaker than a trial but was checkable by others who adopted the method and reported the same fall. The spray was later abandoned — it poisoned surgeons and was unnecessary once the focus moved to sterilising instruments and hands rather than the air.

title: The Periodic Table
detail: Arranging the elements by atomic weight, Mendeleev finds properties repeat at intervals — and where the pattern breaks he leaves gaps rather than forcing a fit, predicting the weight, density and chemistry of elements nobody had found. Gallium, scandium and germanium turned up within fifteen years, matching his specifications closely.
evidence: The gaps are what make this science rather than filing. A classification that merely organises known things cannot be wrong; one that specifies the properties of things not yet discovered can be, and this one was checked three times and passed. He also reversed two pairs against their weights because the chemistry demanded it, which atomic number later vindicated.

title: The Meiji Restoration
detail: Japan, closed for two centuries, responds to the arrival of American warships not by resisting industrialisation but by adopting it deliberately and at speed — sending missions abroad to study railways, law, medicine and navies, and rebuilding its institutions from selected foreign models. Within forty years it defeats a European great power at sea.
evidence: The Iwakura Mission of 1871–73 is unusually well documented: fifty officials, including half the government, travelling for twenty-two months through the United States and Europe, with a five-volume official report recording what they chose to adopt and what they rejected. It is a written record of a country deciding what to become.

title: Koch's Postulates
detail: Pasteur showed that microorganisms cause disease in general; Koch supplied the rules for proving which organism causes which. Find it in every case, grow it in pure culture, give the disease to a healthy animal with that culture, then recover it again. He identified the causes of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera, and invented the agar plate for growing them.
evidence: The postulates are a standard for evidence rather than a discovery, and their limits are instructive: some pathogens cannot be cultured, some infections are asymptomatic, and viruses were unknown. They have been revised repeatedly since — but the demand that causation be demonstrated rather than asserted is the part that stuck.

title: Michelson–Morley
detail: If light is a wave in a medium filling space, the Earth's motion through it should make light travel at different speeds in different directions. Michelson and Morley split a beam, sent the halves along perpendicular arms on a stone slab floating in mercury, and looked for the shift when it rotated. There was none — not a small one, none.
evidence: It is the most famous null result in physics, and its significance is that the apparatus was sensitive enough for the absence to mean something: the expected shift was about forty times their detection threshold. Repeated with greater precision ever since, always null. Einstein later said it was not what led him to relativity, though it removed the alternative.

title: Votes for Women
detail: New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country to grant women the vote in national elections, after a petition gathered nearly thirty-two thousand signatures — about a quarter of the adult European women in the country — and was unrolled across the floor of parliament on a length of wallpaper. Other countries took another twenty-five to fifty years.
evidence: The petition survives and is held in the national archive, with the signatures readable, which makes the scale of the campaign a matter of record rather than recollection. Māori women were included from the start, which was unusual; the property qualifications that excluded many women elsewhere did not apply.

title: X-Rays
detail: Working with a discharge tube wrapped in black card, Röntgen notices a screen glowing across the room. Something is passing through the card, and through wood, and through flesh. Within weeks he has photographed the bones of his wife's hand, and within a year X-rays are in hospital use worldwide. He refused to patent it.
evidence: He spent seven weeks testing before announcing anything, working alone and ruling out known radiations, which is why the first paper stood up immediately. The speed of adoption is itself documented — a surgeon in Birmingham used one to locate a bullet within four months of publication.
facts: 1895, by accident, then tested for 7 weeks

title: Radioactivity
detail: Marie Curie finds that the radiation from uranium is proportional to the amount of uranium and unaffected by heat, light or chemical state — so it comes from inside the atom, which was supposed to be indivisible. Measuring pitchblende, she finds it more active than its uranium content allows, and reasons there must be unknown elements in it. She and Pierre processed tonnes of ore to extract a tenth of a gram of radium.
evidence: The inference to new elements came from a quantitative discrepancy, not from a chemical hint — she trusted her electrometer measurements over the assumption that the ore contained only what was known. She named the field, won Nobel Prizes in two sciences, and her notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection.
facts: Radiation comes from inside the atom
Polonium and radium, from a discrepancy

title: The Quantum
detail: Classical physics predicted that a hot object should radiate infinite energy at short wavelengths, which it obviously does not. Planck found the formula that fits the measured curve by assuming energy is emitted in discrete packets proportional to frequency. He regarded it as a mathematical trick and spent years trying to get rid of it. He could not, and it was true.
evidence: The formula was fitted to Berlin laboratory measurements of black-body radiation that were more precise than anything before, which is why the discrepancy could not be waved away. Einstein took the packets literally in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect, and that — not relativity — is what his Nobel Prize was for.
facts: A trick he hoped to remove

title: Powered Flight
detail: Two bicycle makers succeed where better-funded rivals failed because they identified the real problem as control rather than power. They built a wind tunnel, tested two hundred wing shapes, found the published lift tables were wrong, and worked out three-axis control by warping the wings. The first flight covered thirty-seven metres and lasted twelve seconds.
evidence: Their wind tunnel data survives and can be compared against modern values; it is remarkably good, and finding that Lilienthal's widely used coefficients were in error was the step that made the aircraft possible. The four flights of 17 December 1903 were photographed and witnessed by five people, which is why the date is not in dispute.

title: Special Relativity
detail: A clerk in a patent office publishes four papers in one year: the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and the equivalence of mass and energy. Relativity begins from two premises — the laws of physics are the same for everyone moving steadily, and light's speed is the same for everyone — and concludes that time and length are not absolute.
evidence: The Brownian motion paper is the underrated one: it gave a quantitative prediction for the jiggling of pollen grains, confirmed by Perrin in 1908, which finally convinced the remaining sceptics that atoms exist. Time dilation is now measured routinely — GPS satellites would drift by about ten kilometres a day without the correction.

title: The Nucleus
detail: Firing alpha particles at gold foil, Geiger and Marsden found that about one in eight thousand bounced almost straight back. Rutherford said it was as if you had fired a shell at tissue paper and it came back at you. The atom is almost entirely empty, with nearly all its mass in a tiny, dense, positively charged core.
evidence: The quantitative scattering distribution is the argument: a diffuse charge cannot produce large-angle deflections at all, and the measured angular distribution matches a point charge precisely. It also gives an upper bound on the nucleus' size, about ten thousand times smaller than the atom — a number extracted from counting flashes on a screen in a dark room.

title: Leavitt's Law
detail: Employed to measure star brightnesses on photographic plates at thirty cents an hour, Henrietta Leavitt notices that among variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds, the brighter ones pulse more slowly — and since they are all at roughly the same distance, the relation must be intrinsic. That turns a Cepheid's period into its true brightness, and comparing true to apparent gives distance.
evidence: It is the first reliable measuring stick beyond our own neighbourhood, and everything about the scale of the universe rests on it: Hubble used Cepheids to prove that Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way, and then to find the expansion. She was not permitted to operate a telescope, and she died before the consequences were understood.

title: Continental Drift
detail: A meteorologist points out that the coastlines fit, that the same fossils and rock sequences continue across oceans, and that glacial deposits in India and Africa make no sense unless the continents have moved. He was right about the fact and wrong about the mechanism, proposing forces far too weak, and geologists rejected the whole thing for fifty years.
evidence: He assembled evidence from four independent fields — geodesy, geology, palaeontology and climatology — and the convergence is what makes the case strong in hindsight. It was accepted only in the 1960s, when seafloor magnetic stripes supplied the mechanism he lacked. He died on the Greenland ice sheet in 1930, decades before vindication.

title: Haber–Bosch
detail: Nitrogen makes up most of the air and almost nothing can use it. Haber found conditions under which it combines with hydrogen to make ammonia, and Bosch built the plant to do it at scale. Synthetic fertiliser now supports roughly half the people alive; about half the nitrogen in your body passed through this process. Haber also directed Germany's chemical weapons programme.
evidence: The dependency is measurable by isotope: industrial ammonia carries a distinct nitrogen signature, traceable into crops and into human tissue. The same plants made nitrates for explosives, which is why the blockade of Germany did not end the First World War quickly. His wife, herself a chemist, shot herself days after the first gas attack.
facts: By nitrogen isotope, into our bodies

title: Ramanujan
detail: A shipping clerk with almost no formal training sends a letter of unproved theorems to Cambridge. Most recipients ignored it; Hardy realised no one could have invented such results without knowing they were true. Ramanujan's notebooks contain thousands of formulas, many stated without proof, some wrong, and some not understood until decades after his death at thirty-two.
evidence: A notebook lost for fifty years was found in 1976, and its results on mock theta functions turned out to be connected to black hole entropy — a use he could not conceivably have imagined. His formula for pi converges so fast that eight digits arrive per term, and it underlies modern high-precision computations.

title: Noether's Theorem
detail: Every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity. Symmetry in time gives conservation of energy; in space, momentum; in rotation, angular momentum. The great conservation laws stop being separate empirical facts and become consequences of the shape of the laws themselves. It underpins essentially all of modern theoretical physics.
evidence: It was proved to resolve a specific puzzle Hilbert and Klein had run into with energy conservation in general relativity, and it answered it completely. Noether was refused a paid position for years because she was a woman; Hilbert reportedly asked the faculty whether the senate was a bathhouse. She was dismissed in 1933 and died in exile two years later.
facts: On grounds of sex, for years

title: The 1918 Influenza
detail: An influenza pandemic infects perhaps a third of humanity and kills somewhere between seventeen and a hundred million people in about two years — more than the war that helped spread it. Unusually, it killed healthy young adults disproportionately, apparently by provoking an overwhelming immune response. It was not Spanish; Spain was neutral and its press uncensored, so its reports were the ones anyone read.
evidence: The virus was sequenced in 2005 from lung tissue preserved in formalin since 1918 and from a body buried in Alaskan permafrost, and reconstructed under containment. It was an H1N1 avian-derived strain. The age profile is visible as a W-shaped mortality curve, against the usual U shape of influenza.

title: The 1919 Eclipse
detail: General relativity predicts that the Sun's gravity bends starlight by twice the amount Newton's theory allows. The only way to see it is during a total eclipse, with the stars near the Sun visible. Eddington took an expedition to an island off West Africa, and a second went to Brazil. The measured deflection matched Einstein, and he became famous overnight.
evidence: The Príncipe plates were poor — it rained most of the morning — and Eddington's decision to discard one instrument's data has been debated ever since, with some arguing he favoured the answer he wanted. Reanalysis of the original plates in 1979 supported the conclusion, and the effect has since been measured to far higher precision by radio astronomy.

title: Penicillin
detail: Fleming returns from holiday to a stack of culture plates, one contaminated by a mould with a clear ring around it where the bacteria have died. He identifies the mould and publishes, then largely moves on — he could not purify enough of the substance to be useful. Ten years later Florey and Chain in Oxford did, and turned a curiosity into the drug.
evidence: The famous plate survives. The mould strain was a rare one, apparently drifted up from a laboratory below, and the cool spell that let it grow before the bacteria took over was unusual for London in September — a chain of accidents that has been reconstructed in detail. The first patient treated in 1941 recovered, then died when the supply ran out.
facts: Recovered, then the supply ran out

title: The Expanding Universe
detail: Using Leavitt's Cepheids, Hubble shows that the spiral nebulae are galaxies far outside our own — the universe is vastly larger than anyone had assumed. Then he finds that the further a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. Space itself is expanding, which implies it was once much smaller, and therefore that it had a beginning.
evidence: The recession comes from redshift measured spectroscopically and distance from Cepheids, two independent methods plotted against each other. His original distances were off by about a factor of seven because of an error in the Cepheid calibration, so his expansion rate was badly wrong — the relationship held, the number did not. Lemaître had derived the same result two years earlier.

title: On Computable Numbers
detail: Asked whether there is a mechanical procedure that can decide any mathematical statement, Turing invents an imaginary machine — a tape, a head, a table of rules — to define what a mechanical procedure even is, and then proves that no such machine can decide whether an arbitrary program will halt. The answer is no, and the by-product is the definition of a computer.
evidence: The proof is by a diagonal argument: assume such a machine exists, then construct a program that contradicts it. It is a theorem, so it does not need experimental support — but the machine model turned out to describe every computer built since, and Church had reached the same conclusion by different means months earlier.
facts: Can every statement be decided mechanically?

title: Nuclear Fission
detail: Hahn and Strassmann bombard uranium with neutrons and find barium, which should be impossible — barium is far too light. Meitner, a refugee from Nazi Germany, works out with her nephew during a walk in the snow that the nucleus has split in two, and calculates the energy released from the mass difference using Einstein's relation. It comes to about 200 million electronvolts per atom.
evidence: The chemistry was Hahn's and the physical explanation Meitner's, worked out by correspondence because she had fled and could not be credited in a German journal. Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize. Element 109 was named meitnerium in 1997.

title: Colossus
detail: The first programmable electronic digital computer, built with fifteen hundred valves to break the German high command's teleprinter cipher. It read punched tape at five thousand characters a second. Ten were running by the war's end. They were then broken up, the drawings burned, and everyone involved bound to silence for thirty years.
evidence: Because of the secrecy, ENIAC was credited as the first electronic computer for decades and the British machines are absent from the early histories. Enough documentation survived, along with veterans' memories, for a working rebuild to be completed at Bletchley in 2007. Tommy Flowers, who designed it and part-funded it himself, was never properly compensated.
facts: With drawings burned, after the war

title: The Columbian Exchange
detail: Two biological worlds that had been separate since the continents parted are joined in a few decades. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and cacao go east; wheat, cattle, horses and sugar go west. So do diseases, against which the Americas had no immunity, and the population of two continents falls by something on the order of ninety percent. It is the largest and fastest reorganisation of life on Earth that people have caused.
evidence: The demographic collapse is estimated from colonial tribute records, archaeological settlement counts and modelled disease mortality, and the figures are wide. One striking line of evidence is atmospheric: ice cores record a dip in carbon dioxide around 1610, consistent with farmland across the Americas reverting to forest after the people who worked it died.

title: Burning the Carboniferous
detail: Coal is not fuel in the ordinary sense; it is three hundred million years of buried sunlight, and burning it releases in a century what took a period to accumulate. That is what breaks the ceiling every previous society had lived under, where the available energy was whatever the sun delivered that year. Everything downstream — the population curve, the cities, the atmosphere — follows from taking energy out of the past.
evidence: Coal output and steam-engine numbers are recorded directly in commercial and tax records from the outset. The atmospheric consequence is measured in ice cores, where carbon dioxide is flat for the previous ten thousand years and then begins to climb from this point, and in the isotopic signature of that carbon, which is unmistakably fossil.
facts: Fossil carbon, in the ice cores

title: Trinity
detail: The first nuclear detonation, in the New Mexico desert. It marks the point at which a single species acquires the ability to alter conditions across the whole planet deliberately and quickly — and it left a physical marker everywhere, because the atmospheric testing that followed spread radioactive isotopes into every soil, ice sheet and living body on Earth.
evidence: That marker is why this moment is a candidate boundary for a formal geological epoch: plutonium-239 and a carbon-14 spike appear simultaneously in sediments and ice worldwide, which is exactly the kind of globally synchronous signal a stratigraphic boundary requires. The proposal to formalise it was rejected in 2024, but the signal is not in dispute.

title: The Keeling Curve
detail: From 1958 one instrument on the side of a Hawaiian volcano measures atmospheric carbon dioxide continuously. Within a few years it shows two things at once: an annual sawtooth as the northern hemisphere's forests leaf out and die back — the planet breathing — and beneath it a relentless rise. It is the single most consequential dataset ever gathered, and it exists because one person kept the funding alive for decades.
evidence: Its power is in being one continuous, calibrated record from one place rather than a reconstruction. It agrees with ice-core measurements where they overlap, which is what ties the modern instrumental record to the eight-hundred-thousand-year one and shows that the current level is outside anything in that entire archive.
facts: The annual breath, and the rise

title: Leaving
detail: Something that evolved on the African savanna stands on another world. What came back mattered more than what went: the photograph of Earth taken from lunar orbit the previous year showed the whole planet at once, with no borders visible on it, and is generally credited with doing more for the environmental movement than any argument. The instruments left on the surface are still being used — laser reflectors that measure the Moon's retreat to within millimetres.
evidence: Independently confirmed by the reflectors themselves, which any sufficiently equipped observatory can bounce a laser off, and by returned lunar samples whose composition matches no terrestrial rock. Those same reflectors give the 3.8 centimetres per year figure that appears on the cosmic scale of this map.

site: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey
title: The Transistor
detail: A sliver of germanium with two contacts amplifies a signal, doing the work of a vacuum tube with no heat, no vacuum and a fraction of the size. Everything digital follows from it. Around thirteen sextillion have now been manufactured, which makes it by an enormous margin the most-produced artefact in human history.
evidence: The laboratory notebooks, signed and witnessed daily for patent purposes, record the 1947 demonstration precisely. Shockley's junction transistor, conceived partly out of resentment at being left off the first patent, was the design that proved manufacturable — the point-contact device of the original demonstration was not.

title: Information Theory
detail: Shannon defines information as the reduction of uncertainty, measures it in bits, and proves that any message can be sent over any noisy channel with arbitrarily few errors, provided you stay under a calculable capacity — and that this is impossible above it. He also separates meaning from transmission entirely, which is what lets one theory cover speech, images and text alike.
evidence: The capacity theorem is a proof, and it sets a hard limit that engineering has been approaching ever since: modern error-correcting codes reach within a fraction of a decibel of the Shannon bound. He arrived at it partly through wartime cryptography work, and the same paper introduced the word 'bit' in print.
facts: A hard limit on every channel
Reach within a fraction of it

title: Partition
detail: British India is divided into two states along a boundary drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India and was given outdated maps and census figures. Between ten and twenty million people move, in the largest migration in history; between several hundred thousand and two million are killed. The line still generates conflict.
evidence: Radcliffe burned his working papers before leaving, so the reasoning behind specific decisions cannot be reconstructed — the documentary record of one of the twentieth century's most consequential lines was deliberately destroyed. Death tolls rest on later demographic reconstruction from census gaps rather than any contemporary count.
facts: Five weeks, by a first-time visitor

title: The Double Helix
detail: Two strands wound around each other, with bases pairing across the middle — A to T and G to C — so that each strand carries the template for the other. The structure explains heredity at a stroke, and Watson and Crick said so in a famously understated closing sentence about a possible copying mechanism.
evidence: The decisive datum was Photograph 51, an X-ray diffraction image taken by Raymond Gosling in Rosalind Franklin's laboratory, showing the helical cross pattern and giving the dimensions. It was shown to Watson without her knowledge. Franklin's own unpublished report had already deduced much of the geometry; she died in 1958 and the Nobel Prize came in 1962.

title: Sputnik
detail: A polished metal sphere fifty-eight centimetres across, with four aerials and a radio beeping on a frequency anyone could receive, becomes the first human object to orbit the Earth. Amateur listeners worldwide could hear it, which was deliberate. It burned up after three months, having reordered the politics, funding and self-image of two superpowers.
evidence: The orbit was tracked by radio and optically from many countries, so the achievement was independently verifiable within days — a form of public evidence chosen for that reason. Tracking its Doppler shift to determine its orbit led directly to the inverse idea, fixing a receiver's position from known satellites, which became GPS.

title: Cloning
detail: A lamb is born carrying the genome of an adult ewe's mammary cell, showing that a fully specialised adult cell can be reset to make an entire organism. The assumption that development was a one-way street had stood for a century. Dolly took 277 attempts and was the only live birth.
evidence: Her identity was confirmed by DNA fingerprinting against the donor cell line, which was necessary because the claim was so unlikely. The result directly inspired the work on reprogramming adult cells with defined factors, which won a Nobel Prize in 2012 and removed the need for embryos entirely.

title: The Green Revolution
detail: Dwarf wheat and rice varieties, bred to put energy into grain rather than stem and to stand up under heavy fertiliser, roughly double yields across South Asia and Latin America within two decades. India goes from importing grain to exporting it. The famines confidently predicted for the 1970s and 80s did not happen.
evidence: The yield gains are recorded in national agricultural statistics and are unambiguous. The costs are equally documented: dependence on fertiliser and irrigation, aquifer depletion in the Punjab measurable from satellite gravity data, loss of crop diversity, and benefits skewed toward farmers who could afford the inputs.

title: Plate Tectonics
detail: Wegener's continents finally get their engine. Magnetic surveys of the seafloor reveal symmetrical stripes either side of the mid-ocean ridges, recording the Earth's field reversals as new crust forms and spreads outward. The ocean floor is a conveyor belt, and within a few years the whole of geology is rebuilt around it.
evidence: The stripes are the proof and their symmetry is what makes them unanswerable: any explanation other than spreading has to account for a mirror image about the ridge. Dating confirmed it — seafloor age increases with distance from the ridge, and nowhere on Earth is oceanic crust older than about 180 million years.
facts: All of geology, within a decade

title: The Echo of the Big Bang
detail: Two radio engineers cannot get rid of a persistent hiss in their antenna. They check everything, evict a pair of nesting pigeons and scrub out the droppings, and the noise remains — the same in every direction, day and night. Thirty miles away a group was preparing to look for exactly this: the cooled afterglow of the early universe.
evidence: Isotropy is what made it cosmological rather than local, and the measured temperature matched the prediction. It settled the steady-state versus Big Bang argument decisively, because a steady-state universe has no reason to be bathed in radiation at a specific temperature. Later satellites mapped its tiny fluctuations, from which the universe's age and composition are now derived.
facts: It is the same in every direction
The age and contents of the universe

title: The Pill
detail: An oral contraceptive separates sex from reproduction reliably for the first time, and the effects on women's education, earnings and marriage age are measurable across every country that legalised it. Economists have since tied a substantial share of women's entry into law, medicine and business to the ability to defer a first birth.
evidence: The causal claim is unusually well supported because US states changed the law at different times, giving a natural experiment: outcomes track access, not the calendar. The large trials were run on poor Puerto Rican women who were not told the drug was experimental or that serious side effects had been reported.
facts: On women not told it was experimental

title: The First Network Message
detail: A student types the first two letters of LOGIN to a machine at Stanford and the system crashes. The design decision that mattered was packet switching — chopping messages into pieces that find their own way and reassemble — which means the network has no centre to destroy and no operator to ask permission from.
evidence: The log book records the attempt with the time written in, and it survives. That the architecture was chosen partly for survivability is documented in the RAND reports that preceded it, though the popular claim that it was built to withstand a nuclear war is an overstatement its own designers have repeatedly denied.

title: The Ozone Hole
detail: British scientists measuring Antarctic ozone by hand find it has fallen by a third since the 1970s. Satellites had been recording the same collapse and discarding it, because the software flagged readings that low as instrument error. Within two years the world had agreed to phase out the chemicals responsible, and the layer is now recovering.
evidence: The satellite data was reprocessed after the ground measurements were published and the hole was there all along — a standing lesson about automated quality control discarding real anomalies. The Montreal Protocol is the only UN treaty ratified by every country, and the recovery is measurable: ozone levels are tracking projections.

title: Chernobyl
detail: A safety test at a reactor with a design flaw, run by a crew pushed past the rules, produces a power surge that blows the lid off and burns graphite for nine days, spreading fallout across Europe. The exclusion zone, emptied of people, has since become one of Europe's richest wildlife refuges — which says something uncomfortable about what we do to landscapes.
evidence: The Soviet authorities said nothing for two days. It was detected first by workers arriving at a Swedish nuclear plant whose clothing set off contamination alarms; the plume had crossed the Baltic. The fallout distribution across Europe is mapped in soil caesium-137 and is still used to date sediment layers.

title: HIV
detail: A new immune deficiency is recognised in 1981 and the virus isolated in 1983. It kills tens of millions. Then, unusually fast for a retrovirus, it becomes manageable: combination therapy from 1996 turns a terminal diagnosis into a chronic condition, and people on effective treatment cannot transmit it at all.
evidence: The origin was traced by molecular clock to a chimpanzee virus crossing to humans around 1920 in southeastern Cameroon, then spreading via Kinshasa — a route reconstructed from sequence divergence and confirmed by the oldest known positive sample, a 1959 blood specimen from that city. The untransmissibility of a suppressed viral load was established by trials completed in 2016.

title: Smallpox Eradicated
detail: A hospital cook in Somalia becomes the last person in history to catch smallpox naturally. The disease had killed perhaps 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. It is the only human infectious disease ever eradicated, achieved not by vaccinating everyone but by ring vaccination — finding each case and immunising the circle around it.
evidence: Eradication was certified in 1980 after two years of intensive searching found nothing, with rewards offered for reporting a case. The strategy's effectiveness is quantifiable: ring vaccination broke transmission in India with far less coverage than mass vaccination would have required. The last death was a photographer infected by a laboratory leak in Birmingham in 1978.

title: Lucy
detail: Forty percent of a single hominin skeleton, three point two million years old, showing a creature a little over a metre tall with a chimpanzee-sized brain and a pelvis and knee built unmistakably for walking upright. She settled the order of events: bipedalism came first, and the brain grew long afterwards.
evidence: The completeness is what mattered — isolated bones can be argued about, an associated skeleton constrains the anatomy as a system. She is named after a Beatles song played in camp that night, and in Amharic is called Dinkinesh, 'you are marvellous'. Her species is now known from hundreds of specimens.
facts: Walking came before the big brain

title: Voyager
detail: Two probes leave on a planetary alignment that occurs once in 176 years, tour the outer solar system by slingshotting from one giant to the next, and keep going. Both have now left the heliosphere and are the most distant human objects. They run on about the power of a few light bulbs and still return data, half a century on.
evidence: The gravity-assist trajectory was computed in advance and executed to within kilometres across billions — a direct test of Newtonian mechanics at scale. Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012, confirmed by a plasma density jump rather than by any boundary marker. The Pale Blue Dot image was taken at Sagan's insistence, over objections that it had no scientific value.

title: PCR
detail: A method for copying a chosen stretch of DNA over and over until there is enough to work with — doubling every cycle, so thirty cycles give a billionfold amplification. It makes forensic genetics, prenatal diagnosis, ancient DNA and most of modern molecular biology possible from vanishingly small samples. It is also what a COVID test does.
evidence: The key ingredient was an enzyme from a bacterium living in Yellowstone hot springs, which survives the heating step that separates the strands. That organism had been described in 1969 for no applied reason at all, which makes PCR a standard exhibit for why untargeted basic research is worth funding.
facts: An enzyme from a hot spring
Described in 1969, with no application in mind

title: The World Wide Web
detail: A proposal for managing documents at a physics lab — addresses, a markup language, and a protocol for fetching — is built on top of the existing internet and then given away. CERN placed it in the public domain in 1993 with no licence and no fee, which is the decision that let it become universal rather than one network among several.
evidence: The original proposal survives with his supervisor's note on it: vague, but exciting. The counterfactual is visible in the commercial online services of the period, which were incompatible walled gardens; the web won on being free to implement. Its openness is also why it could be enclosed later by whoever built the most-used layers on top.

title: The Wall Comes Down
detail: A garbled announcement at a press conference implies that travel restrictions are lifted immediately. Crowds gather at the crossings, the guards have no orders and nobody wants to be the one who shoots, and the barriers open. A division that had organised world politics for forty years ends in an evening, partly by accident.
evidence: The press conference is on tape, including the official checking his notes and saying 'immediately, without delay' because he had not been briefed on the intended timetable. Border guard logs and later interviews confirm that the decision to open was taken locally, by officers acting without authority in front of a crowd.
facts: Forty years of division, in one evening

title: The First Exoplanet
detail: A planet is found orbiting an ordinary sun-like star, detected by the tiny wobble it induces. It turned out to be a Jupiter-mass world orbiting closer than Mercury with a four-day year — something no theory of planet formation permitted, which is why earlier surveys had not looked for short periods. Thousands more followed.
evidence: The wobble is measured as a Doppler shift of a few tens of metres per second in the star's spectrum, and was confirmed within a week by an American group who had the data and had not examined it for such short periods. The discovery's main effect was to show that our own system is not the template.
facts: Our solar system is not typical

title: The Human Genome
detail: Three billion base pairs, read end to end, by a public consortium and a private company racing each other. The headline surprise was the gene count: around twenty thousand, far fewer than expected and no more than a nematode has, which ended the idea that complexity scales with gene number.
evidence: The public project released data nightly into the open under the Bermuda Principles, which is why the sequence could not be patented and why the comparison work was possible at all. It was declared complete in 2003 with about 8% still unread — highly repetitive regions that defeated the technology. That last 8% was finished in 2022.

title: A Genome From a Fingertip
detail: A bone fragment from a child's little finger is sequenced, and the genome belongs to neither us nor Neanderthals but to a population nobody had suspected. It is the first time a human group has been identified from DNA before anyone knew what it looked like. Their ancestry survives at its highest levels in New Guinea and Australia.
evidence: The method has since been pushed further: DNA can now be recovered from cave sediment with no bone present at all, showing who occupied a site even where nothing was buried. Screening thousands of unidentifiable fragments by collagen fingerprinting found a bone from a girl whose mother was Neanderthal and father Denisovan — a first-generation hybrid.

title: Gravitational Waves
detail: Two black holes spiral together a billion light years away and the collision shakes spacetime. Detectors in Louisiana and Washington measure the passing ripple as a change in length of about one part in ten to the twenty-first — a thousandth of the width of a proton across a four-kilometre arm. Einstein predicted it in 1916 and thought it undetectable.
evidence: Two widely separated instruments recorded the same waveform seven milliseconds apart, consistent with the signal travelling at light speed, which is what rules out local disturbance. The shape matched numerical relativity templates computed in advance. A 2017 neutron star merger was seen in gravitational waves and then in light by seventy observatories.
facts: Same event seen in waves and light

title: CRISPR
detail: Bacteria keep fragments of viruses they have survived and use them to guide a protein that cuts matching DNA. Repurposed, it becomes a way of editing any genome at a chosen address by supplying a matching guide. It is cheap enough that ordinary laboratories can use it, which is what makes it consequential.
evidence: The system was found by people studying why yoghurt cultures resist bacteriophages — again, no application in view. The first therapies were approved in 2023 for sickle cell disease. In 2018 a scientist in China edited embryos and produced live births, was condemned worldwide and imprisoned; the episode exposed how thin the enforcement mechanisms actually are.
facts: Edited human babies born; enforcement thin

title: The Higgs Boson
detail: The last missing piece of the Standard Model, predicted in 1964 to explain why some particles have mass, is found in collision debris at CERN. Two detector teams worked blind to each other's results deliberately. It completes a theory that has survived every test for fifty years — and gives no clue about the ninety-five percent of the universe it does not describe.
evidence: The claim required five sigma — a one-in-3.5-million chance of arising from fluctuation — a threshold agreed in advance precisely to stop people announcing bumps that vanish. Both experiments reached it independently. The apparatus cost about $5 billion and the analysis involved several thousand people.
facts: A theory covering ≈5% of the universe

title: Photographing a Black Hole
detail: Eight radio observatories from Hawaii to the South Pole observe together, using the Earth's rotation to synthesise a telescope the size of the planet, and produce an image of the shadow of a black hole fifty-five million light years away. The bright ring is light bent around something from which no light escapes.
evidence: The data was too large to send over networks — half a tonne of hard drives was flown to the correlators, including some that had to wait months for the Antarctic winter to end. Four teams analysed it independently with different methods and without comparing results, precisely so that a shared expectation could not produce a shared artefact.

title: COVID-19
detail: A coronavirus spreads worldwide within weeks along air routes, and the response is the first attempt to suppress a respiratory pandemic by coordinated behaviour at a global scale. The genome was published within days of the first sequencing, and a vaccine was designed from that sequence in a weekend — then took eleven months to test and manufacture.
evidence: The mRNA platform worked because of decades of unglamorous prior work, particularly on modifying the nucleosides to avoid an immune reaction — research that was repeatedly rejected for funding and cost its author her position, and won a Nobel Prize in 2023. Excess-mortality estimates, which count deaths against the expected baseline, put the global toll near 20 million.

title: The Webb Telescope
detail: A six-and-a-half-metre mirror in eighteen gold-coated segments, folded to fit a rocket and unfolded through three hundred and forty-four single-point failures, parked a million and a half kilometres out with a tennis-court-sized sunshield. It sees in the infrared, which means it sees the earliest galaxies, whose light has been stretched out of the visible.
evidence: Every deployment step was untestable at full scale on the ground, because the structure cannot support its own weight in gravity — so the confidence came from modelling and partial tests. It launched so accurately that it saved enough fuel to roughly double its expected life. It immediately found galaxies earlier and brighter than models allowed.
facts: It cannot hold its own weight

title: The Question of the Anthropocene
detail: Is the present a new epoch in the geological record? The case is that one species has left a global, synchronous, permanent signal — plutonium from bomb tests, fly ash, concrete, plastic, nitrogen from Haber-Bosch, and the bones of some twenty-five billion chickens, which will be the commonest vertebrate fossil of this layer.
evidence: A working group spent fifteen years assembling the case and proposed a lake in Canada as the reference section. The stratigraphic body voted it down in 2024, on the grounds that seventy years is too short to be an epoch and the boundary too recent to be a formal unit. The signals themselves are not disputed — only what to call them.
